translations.text: As the chief gift, wisdom worthy of the good cause has been given by Christ, the God of all, to the nature of the truly wise,
so you should seek from the perfect wise the speaking of wisdom with reverence, and from the foolish [?] of those who know, listening to the wise in silence.
But now the foolish speak wisdom, while silence [?] of their own and of the wise [?]...
[?] they did not understand that "wise speech is pure silver, but silence is choice gold," as Solomon said.
For when silence is added to the wise, then "their wisdom is praised at the gates," for their tongue is mute toward idle speech and idle toward evil words,

for they made the seeking of the reward their work, and were wise in purity altogether, with righteousness together with worthiness, and with the love of God they sang with understanding, offering prayer continually,
as the apostle says: "Pray without ceasing."
But now as for me, since I am not able to pray without ceasing and am lower than all the foolish, my deficiency does not allow me to keep silent, and I have judged something to be better:
that I should speak worthily of the life of God-clothed men, of our blessed father Gregory and his companions and disciples, by the grace and help of God,
as far as I am able to make known to the hearers what was truly related by the disciples of that saint and by the disciples of his disciples.
And through the intercession of those blessed ones, may I find a twofold consolation for my infirmities by writing these words in this way.
For by the grace of the man-loving Holy Trinity, uncreated in essence,
concerning those who are written, in a way beyond our comprehension, forever in the heavens with the angels in the book of the living, the great desert-dwellers who glory in the holy cross,
those holy fathers who first settled in the glorious deserts of Klarjeti and lived worthily: the courage of their endurance and their labour in purity,
which was pleasing to the Lord, and the many miracles they did in the land of Kartli, have suffered by not being written down, for the reason I mentioned before,
though they ought to have been written down to be told to all from generation to generation forever, so that people yet to be born might praise the Lord on the feast of their commemoration.
But now, through the length of time, their miracles have been given over to the depths of oblivion, along with the good deeds and spotless life of those altogether memorable and wondrous blessed men,
who shone like the stars of the heavenly firmament under this visible and perishable sun.
And now, radiant in spirit, they rejoice in the unending light and always intercede for us, gladdened by receiving what Christ promised,
for in return for their labours they have received joy and a gladness without sorrow, unfailing and inexpressible, in the heavens.
Among these blessed ones there shone forth one full of grace and perfected in wisdom, a great priest, an ascetic who governed well, and one who turned the deserts into cities,
a heavenly man and an earthly angel, the blessed Gregory, spiritual father, leader and builder of Khandzta and Shatberdi,
these two glorious monasteries. He became a model of goodness for all the desert-dwelling fathers of that time as they newly built their monasteries.
He was the son of distinguished, noble and Orthodox parents. He was brought up in the royal house of the great Nerse the eristavi, by the hand of the queen, who served God well,
the wife of Nerse. She had adopted him as her son, because he was also her brother's son.
From his mother's womb his mother dedicated him to God, like Samuel the prophet, and he was raised in fasting like the Forerunner,
for from childhood neither wine nor meat touched his mouth, since he had given his soul to Christ as a dwelling place.
He wore the habit of a monk as well, for he kept away from children's games and from all mixing with people, and he stayed alone in his own lodging, which had been set apart for him.
For this reason they called him "the Recluse."
His quickness in learning was very astonishing, for he quickly learned the Psalter ("David"), the church learning that is taught by voice, and the homiletic learning.
He learned everything in the Georgian language. He also learned to read and write many languages, and he learned the divine books by heart.
He also learned well the wisdom of the philosophers of this world, and whatever good word he found,
he would accept, but what was contrary he would reject. His perfection became famous and was spoken of among everyone.
Yet he scorned the outward wisdom of the world, according to the word of the Apostle: "Has not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?"
His speech was seasoned with the salt of grace. When he spoke, he opened his mouth wisely and kept his tongue in order.
As he grew in age, good virtue also grew in him, for he was not proud like a young man, nor fond of tempting foods,
but of his own accord he would repeat the word of Daniel the prophet: "I will not eat desirable bread."
And so the blessed Gregory, humble in heart and poor in spirit, would take the food of the poor only to strengthen his body,
quiet in conduct and merciful in mind. For the principle [?] (literally "face") of holiness was always planted in his heart, sprouting the meadow of the service of God.
The plant of true faith flourished in his soul, and the fruit of the love of God grew abundant in him.
Through such varied and good conduct this priestly youth lived in a way pleasing to the Lord.
He was impressive in appearance, slender in body and full-grown in stature, entirely good in every way, sound in body and spotless in soul.
Then the rulers who had raised him, his blessed mother and the great multitude of the people wanted this blessed one to be ordained a priest. The princes and his mother said to him:
"Son, wholly good and faithful servant of Christ, behold, the time has come of what was spoken by the prophet David, who says:
'Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, or who shall stand in his holy place? Only one who is innocent of hands and pure of heart.'
And now Christ has found you innocent of hands and pure of heart.
So ascend the mountain of the Lord and stand in his holy place, to offer his holy and bloodless sacrifice, as befits your worthiness and as a hope for our souls and bodies."
But although this blessed one loved the priesthood, he was troubled by their words, and fear fell on him because he was still so young. He said to them:
"You know the power of the divine books. You have understood the canon of the holy catholic Church, as laid down by the holy apostles and the blessed hierarchs:
how much caution the priesthood requires, and complete blamelessness, not only in deed but also in mind and in word.
And although God's long-suffering has taken it upon itself to be patient, for disorderly men who hold the priesthood it would be better
if they had never been counted among men at all than to go into endless punishments forever. But concerning faithful priests, know this:
that the priesthood is greater than all spiritual and bodily glories, for it stands in the place of Christ, the true God, who said to his disciples:
'Blessed are you, for many prophets and righteous men desired to see and hear what you see and hear,
and did not attain it.' You have been made worthy of this. In place of his own priesthood the Lord appointed the apostles as priests,
and after them, one after another, all faithful priests. Through them he entrusted the Christians' hope of salvation to the priesthood,
and he sealed with the priesthood all the miracles, the visions of the prophets and the revelations given to men who saw God.
And now there is no other source of salvation for people except the priesthood, concerning which Paul says:
"Through Christ, by the Gospel, I begot you." And the Lord commands:
"Unless someone is born a second time and receives the holy mystery, he cannot enter the kingdom of heaven." And now I see the honor, and I am afraid of the punishment!"
Then those wise princes answered him and said: "Son, chosen one of Christ, the fear of God is the head of the virtues, as Moses says:
'What does God ask of you, O Israel, but that you fear him?' And as Solomon says, 'the fear of the Lord adds days,' for:
the honour of old age does not come from length of time, nor is it reckoned by the number of days. Rather, a man's understanding is his grey hair, and a spotless life is ripe old age.
And again Job says: "It is not those of many years who are wise, nor do the wise know justice,
but it is the spirit, the spirit of the Almighty, that teaches wisdom." And Christ has given you a good old age of mind.
So now be disobedient no longer. Instead, obey the command of Christ and serve him through the priesthood. He is the eternal priest who suffered for us and gave salvation to us all."
Then blessed Gregory submitted to them, and by the will of God he was ordained a priest, as those who pleaded with him had asked.
This was indeed fitting for his reverent conduct, ordered by the divine canon, and for his constant orthodox faith in the Holy Trinity.
And so the multitude of the people rejoiced when they were made worthy to receive the body and blood of Christ from his holy hand.
Then the princes began to consider making him a bishop, for everyone regarded him as an angel of God and a teacher of the truth, as it is written:
"The lips of the priest shall keep justice, and they shall seek the law from his mouth, for he is the angel of the Lord Almighty."
But when blessed Gregory saw that he was held in worldly glory, his heart was greatly troubled. In response to a divine calling, he resolved to flee his own land in secret,
which led him in the manner of the patriarch Abraham, and like the Israelites in the desert.
But God separated Abraham from the land of an unbelieving people, whereas this man he brought out of a believing and pious land, for this reason:
so that in those empty deserts this unquenchable lamp might shine forth, radiant on that lofty lampstand, with oil that does not fail,
so that at the voice and sound of the trumpet it might be kindled and shine with a mighty spirit,
and might lead the wedding company together with his holy disciples. For by that God-seeing grace, wise and pure, he had understood the unchanging kingdom,
the rule of heaven. Out of zeal to be counted in their ranks, he gave up the changeable honour of the earthly kingdom of mortal men and turned away from temporal and material natures,
so that the timeless light might lead him to the immaterial dwelling and the unchanging glory of the kingdom of heaven.
And in this good purpose and on his journey, with the help of the grace of Christ, he found good companions:
Saba, who was called Saban, his mother's sister's son, the second builder of Ishkhani and its bishop;
and Theodore, builder and father of Nedzvi; and Christopher, builder and father of Kvirike.
Faith joined these four together like members of one body, and divine love made them firm, gathered into one purpose, like a single soul set in four bodies.
Then the blessed Gregory spoke the word of David: "What is good, or what is pleasant, but for brothers to dwell together?"
"For just as Christ spoke of his own dwelling among those gathered in his name, so may the Lord himself be among us,
so that this spiritual [?] of ours in exile may be pleasing, and so that our service may be offered pleasingly before him." And they said:
"May Christ God be spiritually among us, in our brotherhood, in our mission, and in our feeble zeal, according to your words, wise Gregory, so that divine power may dwell among us."
Then, all united as one, they sealed themselves with the mighty seal of the sign of the Lord's precious cross, and with joy they set out on a road they did not know.
Yet they were not ignorant, for the Lord alone led them, seeing their pure heart, their prayer that never ran dry, like a spring, and the stream of their tears.
And he brought them from Kartli first to Opiza.
Now at Opiza there were a few brothers gathered for the love of Christ, since the small holy church of the holy Baptist had been found there.
The name of their superior was Abba George, for he was the third father of Opiza, since Samuel and Andrew had died.
When this blessed Abba George saw the blessed father Gregory and his companions,
he understood by divine insight the grace of their worth and received them with joy, not as disciples but as men higher than himself.
He knew by the Spirit that honour from on high was to be given to them by God.
And for a period of two years father Gregory and his companions stayed at Opiza, in the fierce struggle of monastic labour, as was the rule for monks at that time.
Now Father Gregory wished to live in seclusion alone, for he had heard of the angelic life of the solitaries in the expanse of that desert,
who lived on greens and fruit, in the manner of the princes [?],
and some on a little bread. Of some he had heard the name, and some lived hidden. Holy Gregory would visit all those blessed ones and learn from their good ways of life:
from some, prayer and fasting; from some, humility and love; from some, meekness and freedom from anger;
from some, poverty and lying on the ground, or sleeping sitting up; from some, endurance of infirmity and handiwork done in silence, and virtues like these.
And so, filled with spiritual teachings, he would return to his own dwelling, for he had heard from those holy men that:
"May the world be put to shame by our good conduct."
At that time there was at Khandzta a certain elder, a man living alone, righteous and holy, whose name was Khvedios.
This blessed man saw a vision, not in sleep but while awake. He saw, at that holy place where the holy church of Khandzta is now built,
what seemed to be a cloud of light shaped like a church, which stood there for a long time, and a great fragrance came out of the cloud.
And a voice came to that blessed elder, saying that a holy church would be built in this place by the hand of Gregory the priest, the man of God,
and that the fragrance of his prayers and of his disciples' prayers would rise before God like good incense.
When he saw this vision he rejoiced very greatly and waited for the holy man who had been announced to him, for he was accustomed to seeing visions from God.
In the same way Christ made known to the blessed Father Gregory the worthiness of that elder and of that place, so that he would go to meet him.
At that time, guided by the Holy Spirit, our father Gregory, who was pleasing to God, came to Khandzta, to that holy elder.
When they saw each other they rejoiced greatly and prayed. Then the blessed elder said to him: "Bless me, holy Father Gregory, for you are a priest."
Father Gregory said a prayer, and they greeted each other like dear friends of many years. They sat down with joy, and the elder told him about the earlier vision.
The blessed Gregory said to him: "I thank Christ, who led me, your son, to your dwelling and made me worthy to venerate the footprints of your holy feet, chosen one of God!
From now on may your holy cross be my protection, and may the help of your worthy prayers be a wall around me."
But he said to him: "Rather, may the fruit of your holy prayers and your holy cross always be upon me,
this feeble old man. After a few days you will see me turned to dust, holy one of God.
Although you are younger in years, in deeds you are older than I, for you will be the good shepherd of many of Christ's rational sheep, and the crown and hope of my soul forever.
That is why it was not flesh and blood that brought you from your own land to this barren desert, honored father;
rather, you have as your guide the power of the only-begotten Son of God, the wisdom of the Holy Spirit, and the grace of God the Father,
before which [?] every scheme of the enemy's devices is torn apart, like a spider's web before the wind.
And the evil one knows the terror of your holiness, by which he has been bound like some worthless bird. May Christ crush him completely under your feet, holy father."
But blessed Gregory said to him: "Christ promised his disciples:
'I am with you all the days.' And this was not with you alone, but 'until the end of the world,' with all believers.
That same Lord himself dwells with you, venerable father. Through your prayer, may he grant me victory over the demons and their countless schemes,
And they will give you the kingdom of heaven in return for your labors, according to the word of the Apostle:
"The reward is credited to the worker not as a favor but as what is owed."
After this that good elder said to the holy father Gregory:
"The prophet says: 'Your words are sweet to my palate, sweeter than honey to my mouth.'
But the body needs its food, according to the scripture: '[He] who gives food to all flesh, for his mercy endures forever.'"
Then, as was his custom, he gladly prepared a table from what could be found in his great poverty. They blessed it with thanksgiving and began to eat,
all the while speaking the words that are food for the soul: "Lord Jesus Christ, our God, have mercy on us."
And they took great delight in that small meal, as if it were an abundant feast, for God was among those holy men, joy without end and goodness that never fails. Therefore they said:
"We are not in want. We are full of grace from those treasures that never fail, that are unseen and cannot be stolen."
And when they had eaten, they again began to talk about the life of the soul.
Their conversation went on at length: the day grew dark, and the night passed until dawn without sleep, in their prayer and in singing God's praises.
And at dawn he showed him all the surroundings of Khandzta, and holy Gregory loved it very much. Then he said to the blessed elder:
"Let me go to Opiza and quickly return to my companions whom I left there, so that they may come with me and they too may be blessed by your holy prayers."
When he reached Opiza, he brought his brothers the good news that he had seen that holy elder and that place, a good dwelling given by God. And they quickly went to Abba Giorgi,
the abbot of Opiza, and received his holy blessing and the blessing of all the brothers. Then they joyfully made their way to Khandzta.
They prayed and greeted that holy elder as though he were an angel of heaven. He rejoiced to see those blessed men and said to them:
"You are the fruit of holiness, fragrant plants, beautiful roses, good date palms and olive trees full of fruit,
anointed with the oil of holiness. Seeing you today has refreshed my old age, and my joy has been raised up like the horn of a unicorn.
From now on may this wilderness rejoice in you, who do the will of Christ, as you are planted in it." And they said to him:
"Holy father, you who are like holy Anthony, the honor your words give us is beyond our nature,
But may Christ the almighty confirm that gracious word of praise; that is enough for us.
And may the Lord be pleased to give us this grace: to serve your holiness worthily until the end, O holy man of God."
Then the elder said to them: "Even though your hearts are glad to serve me in my old age, know this:
by God's will I will serve myself until my death, for David says: 'Vow and pay your vows to the Lord your God.'
Now I have vowed to the Lord to live alone until my end. In spirit, though, I am with you, and now I must fulfil my vow in deed."
After this he said to the blessed Gregory: "You who are like Elijah and John, blessed among men, there is a small cave near us.
Take me there, you and your brothers, so that I may spend the rest of my days in it, for I have only a little time left in the flesh.
But promise me this: that until my death you will not grow numerous in this place."
And he made the sign of the cross over his own dwelling, and his word prevailed.
And they no longer dared to argue, but went with him to the cave and prayed.
And the elder said: "This is my resting place for ever; here I will dwell, for I have desired it."
Then they kissed one another, and those blessed men bade peace to the holy man and went down to the place that God had appointed for a monastery.
And holy Gregory, with a contrite mind, with tears and outstretched hands, spoke this prayer:
"In this time of our exile and poverty, O Christ, we shall not fear evil, for you,
Lord, are with us, and you have prepared for us this good place of rest according to your will,
in which we shall always offer up supplication in view of that awaited day of your second coming in glory, O God!
Then the dread of terrible things and the roar of the trumpet will make all creatures tremble,
for they will announce to sinners those endless torments, and proclaim to the righteous the good news of endless life.
Then all the tribes of the earth will beat their breasts because of this, for all the guilty will be handed over to scourgings and torments.
And the righteous will mourn for them, for your dread brings trembling even to the blameless. I tremble at it,
for I am unprepared. It is not the shadows of ignorance that have held me back; rather, I have been overcome by the assaults of negligence. So I cry out with sighing:
when the dissolution of bodies comes, and the exposure of sins, and then the renewal and reunion of soul and body,
some to eternal life and others to eternal torment, where then will I find deliverance from the penalty for my sins?
For I have not gained works by which I might be found blameless before your thrones, O Christ!
But through the intercessions of our Lady, the ever-virgin Mother of God, and of all your saints, O merciful Lord and good King,
have mercy and save us together with your chosen ones, so that together with them we may give you glory for ever. Amen."
After this he began building Khandzta, and he ordered the brothers to recite these verses from the psalms of David:
"Of your mercies, Lord, I will sing forever; from generation to generation I will declare your truth with my mouth, for you said: 'He will build up the world with mercy.'"
"And your fields will be filled with richness. You will enrich the beauty of the wilderness, the hills will be clothed with joy, and the valleys will multiply the wheat of the service of God;
they will cry out and sing." So let our mouths say: "Look upon your servants, Lord, and upon the work of your hands!
Guide their sons! Let your light, the light of the Lord our God, be upon us!
'Prosper the works of our hands upon us, O Lord, and prosper for us the work of our hands,'
for we lifted up our eyes to these wildernesses and mountains, from where you came to help us."
"Truly our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth and all created things."
Together they made the sign of the cross over that place and began work to level the ground for the cells, for the rock of Khandzta is harder than that of any of the deserts of Klarjeti.
They prepared that place with great labour, for they had no axe or pick, nor any other such tool.
But the fathers of Opiza gave them everything they had on hand and helped them with every kind of tool and with food for the body.
For at that time no other monastery had been built in those lands except Opiza, and no secular laypeople lived nearby either, because those lands were only newly being settled.
For in Klarjeti and in Tao, in Shavsheti and in all the neighbouring lands, only a few settlers were to be found, here and there in the forests.
The blessed father Gregory first built a wooden church, and after that his own dwelling, then a small cell for each of the brothers, and one large cell to serve as a [?].

The brothers grew in number day by day, for labourers of the eleventh hour joined the Lord to work in the true vineyard. They became companions of those first righteous ones and sharers with the holy martyrs,
When they took courage in the struggle of monastic life, like the holy martyrs and even more than they,
for the martyrs bore witness at only one moment, but these bore witness at every moment for the name of Christ, as David says:
"For your sake we are being killed every day." And Paul says: "Every day I die for Christ."
If the struggle of the saints had not been unceasing, they would not have called that struggle a daily death.
"For the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh, and these are opposed to each other," in the words of the apostle.
For "one breath of a spirit becomes grace within us, and another breath of a spirit becomes sin within us."
For this reason Paul gives the name 'opposing angel' to the human mind.
And just as he preaches about himself, so he speaks about everyone: at times the mind of the holy angels is found in us, and at times the mind of the demons.
For this reason Christ commanded the apostle Peter: "Forgive the brothers not only seven times in a day, but seventy times seven."
These venerable fathers fought powerfully against such passions, both hidden and open, and against the schemes of the adversary, enduring many kinds of hardship and sorrow for Christ.
At that time the blessed elder Khvedios was very old and close to departing from the body.
Then our holy father Gregory came, with the brothers who were with him, to see the elder.
And when they greeted him, they said to him: "Bless us, holy father, for now you are going to the Lord." And he said to them:
"May the God of peace, love, and love for humankind be with you always. But pray for me,
holy fathers, for today I am going to a strange camp and to the awesome thrones of God." And they said to him:
"You are no stranger to that camp of the holy angels, with whom you always rejoice in spirit before Christ,
"But do not forget us, the dwellers of your holy place and the plants of your grace." And he said to them:
"Into the hands of God I commend my soul, and into your hands my body. And by the will of God may our joy be together forever."
And the blessed elder fell asleep, and his passing was sweet to him.
The place was filled with fragrance and with the singing of the holy angels, who carried him away with joy before Christ.
Father Gregory and the brothers brought out his body, clothed in victory, and with holy chanting they buried it in the tomb.
They gave thanks to Christ, who grants victory to those who do his will and crowns them.
Then, by the will of God, the brothers who served Christ grew in number.
Father Gregory would accept none of the negligent. He would first test each one in every good work,
and if he found him pure of heart, without guile, obedient in humility without complaint, and eager for every good work,
he would receive him with joy. For this reason all his disciples were very good and worthy to take up his holy virtues.
And they resembled their good teacher, just as their teacher resembled Christ, who says:
"It is enough for the disciple to be like his teacher." And so they lived well spiritually, but in the body they were in great hardship.
At that time the ruler of these lands was the God-serving great sovereign, the Bagratid Ashot the Curopalate,
a man of right faith, because of whom rule over the Georgians was established for him and for his sons until the end of time.
Holy Gregory was not known to that sovereign or to his sons, those great sovereigns.
There was a certain great nobleman at the court of Ashot the Curopalate whose name was Gabriel Dapanchuli. His family is now called the Dapanchulis.
This nobleman was adorned with every perfection and with wealth, wisdom, stature and courage. He was praised for his success in every undertaking and for his right faith.
He owned some villages near the dwelling of blessed Gregory. When Gregory saw the poverty of his disciples, he came by the will of God to the house of Gabriel Dapanchuli.
Gabriel was not at home, but his God-loving wife Mary met our father Gregory with faith. She honoured him fittingly and sent him away with many good things.
And he brought men with him to be taught, and said to him:
"Holy father, teach these men the way of your monastery. And do not worry about providing for your spiritual children,
For you shall lack nothing from our house; only remember my lord Gabriel and me, your handmaid, and our children in your holy prayers."
And so Father Gregory came back to his monastery with joy, and the brothers rejoiced greatly, for God honors those who glorify him.
When Prince Gabriel came home, his God-loving wife told him that the blessed Father Gregory had come,
and how she had sent him off with joy. When that noble lord heard this, he gave thanks to God for the holy man's visit to his house,
and he blessed his wife. At once he wrote a letter of entreaty and sent good men, asking him to come to his house again.
Our blessed father Gregory obeyed his words and went with the men who had been sent.
When Gabriel, the king's noble, heard that the blessed man was coming, he rose and went out to meet him.
He bowed down before him with joy and eagerly kissed his holy hands. Then he brought him to his house with honor and let him rest there for many days.
He presented his four sons to him. They were thoroughly good and in every way like their father Gabriel: Patrick, Guaram, Arshusha and Abul-Asat.
He said to the blessed Gregory: "Holy man of God, bless them by laying your holy hands on them.
As Israel blessed the sons of Joseph, so bless all our children, together with us, their parents!"
When the holy man saw the great faith of that blessed couple and their children,
he stood up, full of tears of joy, raised his holy hands to God and said:
"Lord, you fulfilled in deed the word of your faithful ones, your saints from ages past, who gave blessings. Now also, Lord,
look upon the prayer of me, your poor servant, and through the prayers of all your saints bless the parents with their children and the children with their parents.
They are true believers and they glorify your holy name.
As you blessed the house of righteous Noah, of the patriarch Abraham, and of all who do your will, O God of glory,
establish that same everlasting blessing among them. Grant them generously the good things of the earth, with length of days, and the endless good things of heaven. And have mercy on us. Amen."
He made the sign of the cross over them all and sat down. Then Gabriel said to the holy man:
"May Christ confirm in deed the word of your lips, worthy father. And may the Lord grant us to serve your holiness with zeal,
so that the Apostle's saying may be fulfilled among us: 'Your abundance supplies their want, and their abundance supplies your want.'"
Now we have bodily goods and you have spiritual goods; let us share these with one another.
Make us partakers in your holy prayers in this life and after death, and count our bones worthy to be laid with your holy bones.
Establish prayer for us in your monastery forever, and we promise you, for our lifetime and for the lifetime of our children:
"To our children's children we are bound in service to you and to your monastery for all ages to come.
"But, holy father, find a good place as a dwelling for women, so that this shall be the rule among us:
if a man of my family becomes a monk, his dwelling shall be Khandzta; and if a woman of my people becomes a nun,
let her live in whatever place in this land you choose and bless.
And just as I have appointed Khandzta for the fathers who have died, so too let the burial place of women who have died be in this newly built house."
Blessed Father Gregory searched diligently and found a good place near Gunatle.
He marked it with a cross, and there they built a convent for women, which is now called the convent of Gunatle.
At Gabriel's request, blessed Gregory arranged for a priest from Khandzta to serve that convent in turns.
Because of this, in keeping with the promise, prayers are offered at Khandzta for all the Dapanchuli to this very day.
Gabriel, the great nobleman, sent Father Gregory on his way with great generosity and gave him masons and all the materials needed to build a church of stone and lime.
So Father Gregory came to his own monastery. His disciples rejoiced, gave thanks to Christ and blessed those who had labored.
Blessed Gregory leveled the site for the church. As he was beginning the church, he spoke this prayer with tears:
"Christ God, as God you revealed to your creatures the plan of your incarnation. The prophets served your kingship in fear by foretelling it,
the apostles by preaching, the martyrs by true confession, and the worthy holy communities in the world and the fathers of the desert by always glorifying your holy name.
And this fourfold divine assembly of all the saints, standing around them like an unshakable wall, has become the strength of your holy churches.
"For you, Wisdom itself, built for yourself a house of holiness where the faithful peoples might entrust themselves to you. And you have called the holy church your body.
Upon your holy name and the name of your saints you built the holy churches and made them firm, so that they cannot be shaken.
For this reason you named the churches after all the saints, so that after the saints died, your flocks would have the churches in their place as their strength and their pride,
your flocks of true Christians, until you come again in glory with the saints.
"Now, Lord, bless this place too, the dwelling of your holy church, by your grace and by the intercession of your saints,
so that I, your poor servant, may be found worthy to build it completely in the name and the unconquerable faith of your great martyr George, who boasted in the cross,
who was brave and gloriously renowned, shining among your holy martyrs and witnesses, whose bodies were cut by the sword but whose faith was not cut off.
Saint George was found to surpass all of them in courage. To Christians who had long been terrified by the lawless, he taught mighty courage
when he joyfully endured many kinds of torture, and, clothed in victory, he was glorified in heaven and on earth.
For this reason the disciples of the blessed ones, together with the holy angels, rejoiced at the completion of his struggles,
for Christ gave him victory over all his enemies, and now also to his relics and his name; and his intercession protects all who glorify him, always and forever."
And he marked the sign of the cross on the site of the holy church, and they began to build.
And so the old church of Khandzta was completed well, by the help of Christ, by the intercession of Saint George, and by the prayer of the blessed father Gregory,
and, in material terms, by the labours of the glorious prince Gabriel and of all the orthodox faithful.
At that time the holy fathers began to build monasteries and holy churches in all those holy deserts, and so the servants of the Holy Trinity, who glorify it always, grew in number.
And the blessed mother Febronia, who was adorned with miracles, came from Samtskhe and settled in Mere.
And there was no limit to the holiness of her life and the spiritual ordering of her conduct.
And through holy, divine love these most blessed people of God, mother Febronia and father Gregory, were of one mind and were friends. And the priest of Mere used to come from Khandzta.
After this, Gabriel the eristavi told the God-serving king Ashot the curopalates about the holiness and the voluntary exile of the blessed father Gregory,

and about how he had built a monastery in the empty desert, and about the virtue of his disciples. He also told him what he had learned from the disciples themselves about the noble standing of that holy man's parents.
When the pious curopalates Ashot understood all this,
he immediately wrote a letter in his own hand and quickly sent it to father Gregory with two men: a good man from among his own attendants and one of Gabriel's servants.
And the blessed father read the curopalates' letter, which was an honourable summons, and he also learned everything from those men.
He set out at once to go before that sovereign, and when he reached the palace, the curopalates' sons came out to meet him.
And when he came to the door of their hall, the curopalates rose and came forward to meet the blessed father Gregory. They greeted one another with great humility and sat down.
And the curopalates said to him: "Holy one, may God's blessing come upon all of us through your mouth." And he said:
"May the mouth of Christ and of all the saints bless you all, for this saying is truly just:
'Where there is the honour of rule, there is the likeness of divinity.' For you, sovereigns,
God has made lords over the governance of the earth, as we see from the good that God does for us through your kingship.
And as the Lord says of Abraham: 'Abraham desired to see my light; he saw it and rejoiced,'
so I too, a poor man, like Abraham, desired to see you and do you reverence. Now I am full of joy, and I offer you prayer as a gift.

May Christ guard your kingship with ever greater glory, in glory and joy. And may he give you, together with your good children, the eternal glory of heaven as your inheritance, with the heavenly powers."
Then the curopalates said to father Gregory: "From time to time God would raise up a prophet for the kings of Israel, to be their pride and a wall protecting the law,
a help to the faithful and a reproof to unbelievers. In the same way, in our times God has revealed you to be the pride of Christians.
so that you may labor for us with your holy prayer before Christ and his saints." But he said:
"O sovereign, you who are called a son of David, the prophet and the anointed of the Lord, may Christ God make you heir to his kingship and also to his virtues. That is why I tell you this.
May rule never be lacking to your sons and their descendants in these lands, for all ages to come,
but may they stand firmer than solid rocks and the everlasting mountains, and may they be glorious forever."
After this, that man, the messenger, spoke in praise of Khandzta, saying:
"That wilderness is good, with bright sun and mild air on every side.
It has a spring flowing abundantly, beautiful, cool and sweet, and a countless multitude of tall trees, and a few other small comforts, as far as such a desert allows.
But fields for sowing and land for mowing there are none at all, nor can there be, on those craggy, harsh peaks of the Ghado mountains."
When the great kuropalates heard this, he donated good lands, and the site of Shatberdi as an estate for Khandzta.
Then the three great sons of the kuropalates, Adarnase, Bagrat and Guaram, each donated generously everything that his monastery needed.
And when blessed Gregory had received those lands and bestowed his blessing on the kuropalates and his sons, he came back to Khandzta, filled with the fruit of many good things,
to his own monastery, and he told the brothers the good news of all that success, won by the grace of Christ and the intercession of Saint George.
They rejoiced, and they blessed the donors for their faith and gave thanks to Christ the benefactor.
And as the monastery grew in material things, so too the number of holy men grew spiritually,

for at that time Father Epiphanius and the priest Matoi came from Kartli, and the great Zenon from Samtskhe. Epiphanius and Matoi had already been friends of this saint, and they came to Khandzta because of his name.
Zenon was the son of a certain prominent man in Samtskhe. He had been brought up in godliness and lived in holiness.
For the fear of God dwelt in him, and he longed for the monastic life, according to the vow made by ascetics.
When his parents died, they left their property to Zenon and to his sister, who lived in the house with him.
Zenon resolved in his heart to leave his father's and mother's property to his sister, to do with as she wished, and himself to become a monk in a foreign land.
While Zenon was planning this, a wicked man, with the help of the devil, seduced his sister, and they went off by night to Shavsheti.
But when Zenon learned of it, he armed himself, alone, mounted a horse and pursued him. And when he had covered a great distance, he said in his heart:
"I am a renowned young man, and the one I am pursuing is utterly contemptible. Even if I overtake him and kill him, it is a snare for my soul,
and if I return home empty-handed, it is a shame for me. Instead, I will now fulfill my vow of monastic life to the Lord."
And this blessed man showed courage, for giving up one's possessions is like shedding one's blood.
He made the sign of the cross over his body, set out on the godly road, and came to Mother Febronia at Mere, for she was of his family.
By the will of God, Father Gregory was there, and Mother Febronia entrusted that innocent lamb to the saint, that good shepherd, who brought him to Khandzta.
He settled in the green place of God's grace, and he raised him beside the restful waters of the Holy Spirit.
This blessed Zenon reached old age, and until the end he did not leave Khandzta. He was truly a spiritual son, like his father,
a good disciple, the successor of his teacher, blessed, a treasury of virtues, a holy rule of monastic life, a wall for the deserts of Klarjeti, and a driver-away of evil spirits,
for during his life and the life of his teacher the devil did not dare to make holy men fall in these places.
Since his death this valiant man has been our intercessor before the Lord for ever, together with his companions, who were like him,
the disciples of Father Gregory. They were worthy men and workers of miracles, unshakable pillars of patience, like the pillars of heaven that are made firm and cannot fall,
for until the coming of Gregory, that good shepherd, the little sheep of Christ were fleeing from invisible beasts and were scattered one or two at a time across the wide desert,
but when holy Gregory came, those sheep took courage, those beasts, the demons, were driven away, and every divine rule was set in order.
Then Father Gregory thought in his heart: "The fathers of my monastery surpass the monks of this time in virtue,
so in the same way it is right that the divine rule of the Church be established in my church, a rule that the wise cannot fault."
So he decided to go to Christ's treasury, the second Jerusalem, which is Constantinople, to visit and pray at all the famous holy places of Greece.
At that time he found a friend of his who was travelling to Jerusalem, and he entrusted him with writing down the rule of Saint Sabas and bringing it back.
He appointed men who were ascetic strivers to lead his brethren, bade them farewell in peace, and promised to come back soon.

He took with him Saba, the son of his mother's sister, and one other disciple. He set out for Greece and reached Constantinople, and there he venerated the Wood of Life and the relics of all the saints.
With joy he went around all the holy places of prayer, for he was trained in many languages and had learned much in the craft of right service.
Some of the things he saw became teachers of good to him, and some became a warning against evil.
In this way his heart was filled with the unsealed riches of the New Law, and, gladdened by the Spirit of grace, they set out for their own home.
When they reached Tao, they heard from the people there that Ashot the curopalates had been killed and that his sons were ruling in his place.
Then they were filled with tears of grief at the fall of that God-serving ruler, and, full of weeping, they prayed for the departed king.
But blessed Gregory gave thanks to God and said, lamenting:
"O my king, mighty and glorious, strength of the churches and rampart of the Christians, from where was I to expect you: from the east or from the west, from the north or from the south?
For you were lord over all peoples, and you subdued rulers in battle, you wondrous, glorious, God-serving ruler!
How then were you handed over to contemptible, lawless and worthless men, who like Judas became the murderers of you, their lord, and brought death on us, your poor intercessors, for ever?"
After this they blessed his sons, the glorious rulers, praying that the Lord would keep them in glory and long life and in good piety.
And as they came near Ishkhani, God revealed to the blessed Gregory and the venerable Saba the former glory of Ishkhani,
and the holy churches in its settlement. And it was made known to them that it was to be renewed again as it had been before, by the hand of Saba.
They were also shown the way to reach it, because at that time people could not get to the place. And when they went to Ishkhani,
they rejoiced greatly at finding that glorious place, because there was consolation in it for both soul and body.
Saba immediately set his heart on staying there, but the blessed Gregory said to him:
"Brother, let us first see our brothers who are at Khandzta. Then by God's will and through their prayers you will come back to this holy place."
As they went on from there, they came before the sons of the curopalate and blessed them, comforting them over the death of their father.
And so they came to Khandzta, their own monastery. They brought relics of the saints, holy icons and a great many other blessed gifts (eulogiae).

They found the brothers alive and at peace, all of them cheerful, untroubled and full of divine love. And they rejoiced, because the grace of the Savior had once again gathered together those who do his will.
A few days later Gregory sent Saba off to Ishkhani and gave him two disciples. He himself directed the spiritual life of Khandzta according to the Lord's will.
Then a man arrived from Jerusalem and brought the rule (typikon) of Saint Sabas and a written text of it.
At that time the blessed Gregory laid down the rule for his own church and monastery,
a rule defined with wisdom, made bright with knowledge and selectively gathered from all the holy places, like a treasury of inexhaustible good things.
Here, however, we have taken up only a small part of those spiritual rules, as if someone were to draw a single drop of water from the sea.
For this was the way of life of those blessed men: for all their righteousness, they always blamed themselves; the root of their love was firm;
they had patience with humility and meekness, and fasting fenced in by prayer and made firm by right faith;
they had purity of heart, truthfulness of tongue and chaste reverence in absolutely everything. In the holy church they did not talk with one another during prayer. Instead they stood in fear,
as if before God in heaven. And when they recited "David" (the Psalms),
until the "Alleluia" was finished, not even the [?] (memkhreta, perhaps the infirm or lame) dared to lift a knee during that calm prayer of theirs,
for they were not in the habit of saying any of their chants quickly. Their prayer was humble and slow.
No one except the elders leaned against the wall, and they never dared to sleep or sit carelessly in the church.
Many other good virtues of this kind were also established among them, but there is no room now to speak of each one in turn,
because time is short and the mind is in a hurry, so that it will not be too much for those listening. For this reason the whole rule could not be written in this book,
only a word or two out of all of it: the rule Khandzta has kept until now and keeps at present, as follows:
At all the vigils there was prayer from evening until dawn. During the vigils there was also prayer at all the hours of the day, the liturgy was celebrated at the ninth hour, and litanies were added.
At every liturgy, the litany "Coming down from heaven" [?] was said before the "Holy God" (Trisagion). At the Sunday liturgy the "Holy God" was said six times.
In the service of the altar, no one dared to serve in [?] garments or in leather.
For all the departed they hold commemorations counted from the death, whatever day it falls on: the third day, the seventh,
the fortieth, and the year. On those days they do not change the liturgy, on those two hundred [?] days appointed for those buried at Khandzta.
The distribution of paximadia (rusks) was established from the very beginning. When the feast of Saint George is set, there is a fast with [?] until the feast of Saint George.
In the same way, they kept the fasts of the Nativity of Christ and of the holy Apostles according to church rule, with great effort and good reverence.
From the beginning of the month of November until the eve of the fast, four canons were sung at matins on every Saturday.
During Great Lent, until Palm Sunday, four canons were sung at every matins, and likewise there were four readings from books.
The Sunday of the Passion had a very elaborate order of service. From the Fulfillment (Easter) until New Sunday, they did not say the canon of tribulation,
and at the Supper (Holy Thursday) they say "At my supper" [?]. Until New Sunday they say the prokeimena of the Resurrection, the hymns appointed for matins, and one canon each.
At the commemoration of souls after the Fulfillment, they say the "Blessed are" (Beatitudes) and hymns at matins. All the rest of this is written in the typikon of the church.
The fathers did all of this in this way in my own times.
But in the early days of our blessed father Gregory, the rule of his disciples was very strict.
For in their cells there was only a small bed, poor bedding, and one jug each for water.
They had no other comfort for the body, and no food or drink of their own at all. They lived only on what they ate together at the table.
Many of them did not drink wine at all.
And those whom they received ate little, and their cells had no chimney, for no fire was kindled,
nor did they light a candle at night. Instead, at night there was psalm-singing, and by day the reading of books, and prayer always, as David says:
"By day the Lord commanded his mercy, and by night his song."
The blessed father Gregory himself passed the great fasts on a little uncooked [?] kalnabi [?].
His double [?] food all his days was bread. He ate it sparingly, once a day, with a little water, also measured by weight.
He had not drunk wine since his youth. Most of his virtues, and those of his disciples, God alone knows.
From the beginning, Theodore and Christopher, the good companions of the blessed Gregory, had in their hearts a divine zeal to build a monastery.
They did not reveal their intention to father Gregory. Instead they went secretly to Abkhazia, and some brothers went with them.
When they reached Samtskhe, by the command of God they took as their disciple the son of the great nobleman Mirean, named Arsenius,
who was rightly called Arsenius the Great, Catholicos of Kartli and the unfading crown of the see of Mtskheta.
The boy was young at the time, about six years old, and was being brought up in his father's house.
But those men of God, on Mirean's advice, dressed the boy in monastic clothing. They gave Mirean their right hand as an oath and said to him:
"Our teacher is Father Gregory of Khandzta. If the Lord wills, this boy too shall be his disciple, with us, wherever we may be."
And they went to Abkhazia. Demetrius, king of the Abkhaz, received them with great honour and settled them in a good place.
When blessed Gregory learned that Theodore and Christopher had gone, he was greatly distressed. He took four brothers with him, and that good shepherd set out to search for those chosen lambs.
When he reached the districts of Kartli, by the will of God, while searching for the brothers, he found the boy Ephrem, a worthy youth,
who in his worthiness was seen to reach full manhood in holiness, and in holiness became bishop of Atsquri, a worker of miracles.
During his time as bishop he reached a good old age and died in a wondrous manner, and his holy relics were given to Samtskhe as a light.
Blessed Gregory took this Ephrem, worthy of God, as his disciple and commanded him thus:
"When I return from Abkhazia, I will take you with me to Khandzta." And he himself set out for Abkhazia.
When he came before that ruler, the king rose, went out to meet him, and greeted him humbly. Awe had seized him because of the grace of Gregory's holiness and the majesty of his face,
for just as the face of Moses the prophet was glorious, so too was the countenance of this blessed man by the grace of God.
After the greeting, the king and blessed Gregory sat down. The saint prayed over him at length and adorned him with many blessings.
And the king said: "Blessed is God, who has led you here, holy father. But what is the reason for your toilsome journey? Tell me."
Blessed Gregory said to him: "God-serving and glorious king, the holy fathers, my brothers, have come
before you and are now in this kingdom. It is for them that I have come here. Let your majesty give the order, and let them come to us."
But the king was displeased by the search for them and said to him: "No such monks as your holiness speaks of have come here."
Then the blessed father Gregory grew angry at the king's words and said to him: "King, do not cause me trouble. Give me my brothers,
who came to you." And since the king had nothing more to say in the face of the saint's just rebuke, he ordered that the brothers be brought.
When they saw Father Gregory, they fell at his feet in tears. The saint raised them up, embraced them with love, and thanked Christ for finding them.
And since those brothers were by nature devoted to and longing for that saint [?], they too rejoiced at being reunited with one another.
And the king said to blessed Gregory: "Holy father, behold, the desire of your will has been fulfilled. Now may the Lord also fulfil the desire of my heart,
for it is in my soul to build a new monastery. Now give the word, and let us look over many places in Abkhazia, and wherever your holiness chooses, let us build a monastery in that place."
And they went around the places thought suitable for a monastery, but none of them pleased the holy man. And he said to the king:
"There is neither land nor water in this country where a monastery could be built, for a monk's talent is fasting,
and in this land fasting is impossible because of the deadly sultry air."
And the king was greatly distressed for this reason and said to them: "It is not right that this land should have no share in your good things."
Then Father Gregory, in accordance with the king's faith, built a monastery and called its name Ube; and a certain Hilarion, who had come from Jerusalem,
a faithful man, he appointed as abbot, for he had gone from Khandzta together with Theodore and Christopher, and he had good books.
And Father Gregory also left to that monastery the books of his own that he had.
And that sovereign was filled with joy over the building of that monastery, and he offered a very great offering for its construction,
and he bestowed on Father Gregory and his companions ten thousand drachmas and filled them with every good thing.
But at the time of their departure, King Demetrius eagerly asked Father Gregory what the wilderness of Klarjeti was like,
so that he would tell him every feature of those holy places. And Father Gregory said to him:
"O king, servant of God, even if I multiply my words greatly, my mind still cannot manage to tell you all the goodness of those deserts,
since the monastic way of life has flourished among them, and it will flourish still more and increase in times to come; but I will tell a little out of much, thus:
"For the land of those deserts is uniform by nature and well tempered in sun and air,
for neither does great heat scorch them, nor does excessive cold afflict those who dwell there.
But it stands in good order within its own bounds, without damp, without humidity, without mud, sunny, so that the footprints of men's feet never become muddy as they walk.

And it has good water, and wood in abundance as one wishes, without lack, growing up among the sands; countless tall forests and a multitude of sweet waters; a natural cheerfulness has been given to it by God.
And it is pathless and in every way inaccessible to those who live by the ways of the world, for their dwelling is among high, rocky mountains.
And on one side the mountain encircles it, and on the other side the course of the confluence of the great waters of Shavsheti surrounds it like an immovable wall.
"And thus they are enclosed on every side by mountains and ravines and by waters, places terribly difficult for those who travel.
And in those monasteries there is no land for mowing hay, nor field for plowing, but with great labor their provisions are brought in on the back of [?].
And they have planted a few vineyards with hardship and anxiety, and likewise gardens; but of the wild herbs of the field there is a countless abundance.
And with all this their heart is without fear of disturbance from the Christless unbelievers, and of every upheaval in times of hostility among rulers.
And thus they live always in much peace and tranquility and glorify Christ.
"For God, at the very beginning of creation, created them for the last times as a dwelling place for monks and a place of refuge for all Christians, in both respects.
And indeed the providence of God has this custom:
that the monasteries of those holy deserts should be built by the hands of the poor, who have become entirely free from the snares of the world.
Although sovereigns take care of the holy desert monasteries, Christ saw fit that the founding of holy monasteries should bear the name of the poor.
But God gave believing kings the authority to build episcopal sees and cities together with villages, and made them rulers over all the people,

so that, adorned in splendid robes, they might judge the people with justice; yet so that they should not leave their minds among these visible things, but should keep the eternal good things in mind.
For divine wisdom, through garments of many kinds, has made known to all people the honour of each of their ranks in the service of God.
"But faithful and true monks are under no one's authority on earth,
since they have willingly turned away from the delights of this passing world and, for God's sake, have chosen affliction in places of mourning, like those first holy fathers,
who lived in great poverty and built the holy desert monasteries without any command from earthly kings, by the help of almighty God.
And now, in our own times too, there are men like those first blessed men, who build monasteries in empty places as dwellings for God,
and pious sovereigns become sharers in their labour by giving wealth generously,
just as today your glorious majesty has enriched our poverty with great goods, and you are fully a partaker in our prayer."
The king rejoiced at the words of blessed Gregory. Great faith and love toward the desert monasteries of Klarjeti were made firm in his heart, and he gave thanks to Christ,
who does good to those who do his will. And so they took leave of that sovereign and came away from Abkhazia.
And as they travelled on their way, the blessed Theodore and Christopher said to blessed Gregory:
"Holy father, when we were coming from Khandzta to Samtskhe, and had come near the estate of Mirian the nobleman,
his men saw us, because at evening we had made our resting place on the plain,
and they told their lord. Mirian himself came at once, greeted us humbly, took us to his house, and gave us good rest.
And when day dawned, he brought us before his lady, whose name is Krava, for she is a handmaid of Christ.
And when we had blessed her and sat down, the glorious lord Mirian ordered his sons to be brought before us: three boys, altogether good and handsome.
And when we had blessed them, he said to Krava: 'Now let us do a good thing as a sign, and dedicate one of our sons as a monk and a disciple of these disciples of Christ,
and through their prayers may grace be given to him, so that those who hate us may see it and be put to shame.
"Now say, which of our sons shall become a monk?" And he said to him:
"My lord, your sons are before you. Whichever one you command, the Lord has chosen him as a chosen monk."
And he said: 'This youngest one shall be a monk and a spiritual son of these fathers of the desert.'
And he brought him with his own hand and gave him to us to sign with the cross, and he clothed him in the garments of monks.
We gave him the name Arsenius, and we promised that his son would be your disciple, as we are. And he rejoiced all the more.
Now do as seems good to your holiness." And the holy one said to him:
"Blessed brothers, it is God's will that by our hands he should become one of the chosen among monks and attain a great measure."
He also told them everything about the worthy boy and youth Ephrem, in the same way as this answer. The brothers rejoiced at their teacher's words.
Together they went to where Ephrem was and brought him away, and the blessed Arsenius as well.
Holy Ephrem was the older of the two. It was about them that the blessed Gregory quoted this saying of David:
"The revelation of God's words gives light and gives understanding to infants." Through these children the praise of Christ would be confirmed.
"Truly these innocent and simple ones have joined us to endure the struggle of the monastic life. They have come according to the Lord's command:
'Do not stop these children from coming to me, for the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these.'
But know this, brothers: our brothers are bound to grumble about us, and with good reason. Yet the Lord himself will care for these children, for he said:
'Take care that you do not cause one of these little ones to stumble, for their angels always see the face of my Father in heaven.'
And now you, brothers Theodore and Christopher, you who are clothed in victory, become good guardians of these children, according to God's will."
They promised to do this and took on the work of caring for the children. Then the blessed Gregory said to them: "Brothers, this is greater than all your other virtues:
keep your eyes on these children at all times. Remember how noble their parents are, and remember their parents' faith in Christ and toward us poor monks.

For the love of Christ, they set aside their love for their children. Through our hands they offered them to the Lord as a sacrifice, and in hope they entrusted them to us, though we are strangers, as if to their own brothers.
Now, just as we have brought them away from their parents innocent, to be kept holy, may Christ find them the same when he asks for them back from our hands as his own inheritance."
When they arrived at Khandzta, the brothers, the holy communities that Christ had gathered, rejoiced greatly at the coming of their spiritual father and of those with him.
But there was murmuring among them about the bringing of the boys. They came before Father Gregory and said to him:
"Holy father, the apostle says, 'Perfect love casts out fear.'"
If your holiness permits it, we will speak without fear about the reason we have come."
And he said to them, "Brothers, truly the love among us is firmly rooted, and there is no fear in it. Say whatever you wish." And they said to him:

"All your deeds are beyond reproach except this: that you bring in these boys. The rule you yourself established will be turned [?] back against you, and in times to come it will be a cause of downfall for us.
Our hearts are not afraid for the present time, but this act goes against the rule. That is what we have to say, holy man of God."
When the blessed Father Gregory heard this good concern, he openly rejoiced and said to them:
"O blessed brothers, far be it from me to change, for any worldly reason, the rule gathered from the early holy fathers.
I speak the truth before God, for you have never heard a false word from my mouth.
This is how these boys came to be here: Christ God made their whole matter known to me through the mouth of a holy angel. For just as Ephrem the Syrian and Arsenius the Roman
were separated from men and drew near to God, so these worthy boys were to be raised spotless in Khandzta until the time of their honour."
"Now then, can we resist the Lord's command? For it is laid upon me even against my will, according to the word of the apostle:
'If I do not preach the gospel, woe is me.' But you are blessed, for the Lord has chosen you for these servants of his.
But if anyone, without such a cause, changes the former rule and brings any boy at all into this monastery,
let him be punished at the most glorious second coming of our Lord and God."
The brothers were convinced and edified by this, and they gave thanks to Christ, the worker of wonders.
Then Theodore and Christopher, whose cells were in one place and apart from the other brothers,
those spiritual fathers, took the God-clad boys to their own cell, according to the command of the blessed father Gregory.
They raised them well by the grace of God, in place of milk.

At that time Bagrat the curopalates, by the will of God, by the will of his brothers, and by the command of the king of the Greeks, received the office of curopalates in place of Ashot the curopalates,
his father, for the power of rule had been given to him from above.
His brothers, all good and glorious rulers, Adarnase the eldest and Guaram the youngest,
submitted to that middle brother out of the love of godly brotherhood, for they were of one mind, one soul and one will.
Bagrat was the foremost of them in wisdom, in appearance and in valour, and in all the joy of serving God,
for in all his piety he was like the prophet David and like the blessed Bagrat (Pancratius), apostle and priest-martyr, disciple of the holy apostle Peter.
By the grace of Christ the kingdom of those three brother rulers was made great.
With the help of God they conquered many lands with their sword and drove out the descendants of Hagar.
The blessed father Gregory came before the glorious Bagrat the curopalates and, as was fitting, congratulated him with an encomium on his becoming curopalates.
The praise of that encomium, beyond the grasp of the wise men of that time, greatly pleased the pious curopalates, and he said to him:
"O holy father, God has adorned you with wisdom, maturity and the Holy Spirit as a wall of salvation for us, a mediator between death and life,
through which you have extended yourself over all this land by your shared care and your godly labour.
I hold love and honour for your fatherhood.
Now let your holiness command from our royal power whatever service befits your dignity, for by God you are a sharer with us, the sons of Ashot the curopalates."

The holy man said to him: "Pious king, more and greater than your pious father, you who are shielded by the wings of the Lord's cross: may the right hand of the Creator and the intercession of the saints always protect you.

"And that sleepless Guardian is always a guardian to you, and the light that knows no night goes before your kingship. It has no need of the brightness of a lamp; that is needed only by those who are in darkness.
"But I have diligently kept up my prayer for you, so that the good work of your kingship may not fail for any cause.
"But now I ask this of you: there is an estate of Ashot the kuropalates, which was donated to Khandzta, and it would make a fine monastery.
"If your kingship commands me, I will build it for the glory of God and for the salvation of your soul. And as long as heaven and earth remain, prayer for you will continue in it."
Then Bagrat the kuropalates joyfully ordered it to be built, and he gave everything needed for the building.
And when the blessed father Gregory went to Shatberdi, the place was watered by a river of his tears as he said this prayer:
"O God, by the sovereignty of your reign you created all creatures without toil, and by your power you govern all your works. For you are the Creator of the heavens,
the Maker of the angels, the One who established the earth and set the seas firmly in place, and you are also the One who does even small things, as David said:
'Unless the Lord builds the house, its builders labor in vain.'
Now, Lord, let your ears listen to the voice of my prayer. Bless this place with your grace, and build a monastery as a place of rest in holiness for those who are your
inheritance. Give it a good and renowned name among many peoples, for your glory, O King of all, through the unseen help of your mighty arm.
And enlighten it with the light of your Holy Spirit, and through the intercession of the holy Mother of God and of all the saints, protect it to the end of the ages. Amen."
And he made the sign of the cross over that chosen place, and they began work on the church and also on the cells.
And so it grew and flourished day by day. And it became a valley of mourning for the enemies, both invisible and visible,
but a harbor of salvation for the flocks of Christ: for kings and princes and for all the orthodox Christian people. Like Khandzta,
which was chosen by God from above, Shatberdi was likewise built by divine help and by the prayers of that blessed man.
He joined those two desert monasteries into one, united as members of one body and made firm in brotherly love until the end of time.
After this the kuropalates summoned the holy man. And when he came before him, he told him about all the good success that the monastery had received through Christ.
Then he granted good lands as an estate for Shatberdi, and he gave him in full everything needed for the building.
At that time the blessed Gregory's heart moved him to recall Saba of Ishkhani, and he told the God-serving kuropalates everything that had happened earlier.
When he heard it, he rejoiced greatly. He quickly wrote a letter, sent good men, and summoned him with honor.
But the envoys came back and told the kuropalates that the man of God did not wish to come here.
Then the kuropalates ordered a journey along the roads to Ishkhani [?], for at that time he was nearby.
And he said to the blessed father Gregory: "I acted thoughtlessly, because I did not have you write a letter. Now write to him, as is proper."
And he himself wrote another letter, and he sent father Gregory's letter as well.
But the blessed Saba obeyed the second command of the curopalates, and even more the letter of his father.
And that beloved man of God went to them, together with those who longed for him.
The kouropalates went out to meet him and greeted him with honour, and he blessed him. When they had sat down, the kouropalates said to the holy man:
"It is right to obey rulers. Why did you not come at the first summons, holy father?"
He replied: "Glorious king, you are ruler of the earth, but Christ is ruler of heaven and earth and the underworld.
You are king of these peoples, but Christ is king of all created things.
You are king in these passing times, but Christ is the eternal sovereign. He abides perfect and unchanging, outside time, without beginning and without end, sovereign of angels and of men.
And it is more fitting to listen to his words than to yours. He commanded:
'No one can serve two masters.' But now, at the word of my brother and teacher Gregory, I have come before you."
The curopalates said: "Your words are just, holy one. But it is better that many souls be enlightened by your shining on the lampstand, since you are a shining lamp.
As Christ said to his disciples, just as the radiance of the sun lights up those who live under heaven,
'so let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father in heaven.'"
After this the curopalates went to Ishkhani, and those blessed men, Father Gregory and Father Saba, went with him.
The curopalates came to love that place greatly. But why should I draw out my account?
By the will of God, Saba was made bishop of Ishkhani, over the cathedral church built by the blessed Catholicos Nerses and over its see, which had been widowed for many years.
Now a spiritual marriage took place once again, and the church was rebuilt a second time: spiritually by this blessed man, and physically through the labors of those God-serving kings.
Whenever Father Gregory came to Ishkhani as a guest, the bishop would seat him on the bishop's throne and sit beside him himself,
for he would not allow himself to disobey the blessed Gregory, since Gregory was his teacher and his superior.
And so Ishkhani has prospered well up to the present day, and will forever.
But now let us return to our earlier account.
Our blessed father Gregory was honored by God from on high, and in his time no one disobeyed his words,
especially not the rulers of that time. There was a time when those glorious brothers were together in one place,
and the blessed man earnestly asked them to be pleased to come and see the monasteries he had built and all the desert retreats of Klarjeti.
They granted the request of that holy man, and he went ahead of the princes to lead them.
First he brought them to Shatberdi. They came to love that place greatly, and the rulers, the nobles and all the people gave many offerings.
Then distinguished nobles came forward as patrons of Shatberdi. And when those rulers set out from Shatberdi, the blessed Gregory went ahead of them.
Then Zachariah, bishop of Ancha, came. He was a worthy man and a worker of miracles. The sovereigns greeted him with honour and took him along with them.
They came to Jmerki and to Berta, to the churches of the holy Mother of God, and to Daba, to the church of the holy martyr George. Dolis-qana became a monastery only later.
They worshipped at the holy places and gave out a great deal in distributions, because the three sovereigns had brought large offerings.
And they received grace through the prayers of these blessed fathers.
Then they came to Opiza. They rejoiced in the grace of the Baptist and in the prayers of those blessed men, and they showed great zeal by giving offerings.
Then they set out for Khandzta. The blessed Gregory brought the abbots of the monasteries along with him, and they came to Khandzta, the dwelling of the great martyr George.
The minds of the sovereigns were amazed even more when they saw the disciples of the blessed Gregory living by the strictest rule of monastic life, for they were like the angels of heaven.
First they received the weapon of victory over their enemies through the intercession of Saint George, and then through the prayers of those blessed men,
and they were enlightened in body together with soul. Because they also saw that the place yielded no produce, they granted it an even greater offering from their wealth.
At that same time the abbot of Midznadzori arrived. This was the great and blessed father David, a builder of monasteries. His disciples came with him, the blessed men:
Hilarion, the father and builder of Tsqarostavi, who also became catholicos at Mtskheta, and father Zachariah, the builder of Bareleti. They came to meet the sovereigns.
When the rulers saw that gathering of holy fathers, who were like the holy bodiless powers, they rejoiced,
because they heard from them teachings on the divine commandment. For this reason the great sovereigns said: "Holy fathers,
since we have seen you, we have completely forgotten that we are on earth. Instead we feel as if we were living in heaven, in the camp of the saints.
For in spirit you always stand before God, and wherever your dwellings are, your hearts are there too. May your intercession be upon us, here and in the age to come."
The holy men armed the sovereigns with many prayers, blessed them and said to them:
"God-serving kings, truly your hearts are in the hand of God. Through your words and through the generous gift of your wealth, he has comforted the hearts of us poor men.
Through your mortal kingship the Lord has granted you to plant holy churches of [or: "for"] the immortal sovereigns.
Their help has invisibly become a weapon for you, greater than visible weapons and stronger than tens of thousands of horsemen.
And know this: these holy men, the fathers of the deserts, are your armies drawn up in the spirit.
They are the strength of your armies drawn up in the body, and they are the weapons of all faithful kings in the ranks of battle.
This is all the more true for you, because together with the height of kingship you have humility like that of Christ and zeal for the holy churches,
and you comfort the poor and judge all the people justly, according to the word of the Lord:
'Do not judge by appearances, but judge with right judgment.' So together with the kingship of this earth, may you also receive an unending dwelling with the King of heaven."
And may Christ give you the full glory of heaven and of earth, so that you may never neglect to remember us with kindness, for the sake of these who dwell in the monastic cells.
Understand that, just as Abraham the patriarch and David the prophet gave the warriors an equal share of the spoils,
so also let the poor and the churches always have a share of your goods, just as the Lord commands concerning the Levites: "I am their portion."
In the same way the portion of the poor has been established by you, so that in return you may gain the Lord as the hope of both lives, for the poor have nothing except the mercy of the good God."
After this the holy fathers took counsel with the bishop concerning father Gregory,
to appoint Gregory archimandrite over all the desert monasteries of Klarjeti, and they reported this to the rulers.
The rulers rejoiced greatly, and together, with earnest entreaty, they appointed him to the work of that ministry.
And for many years, until his death, he governed the rule of those holy fathers well.
Then the rulers made a pilgrimage to Midznadzori, Tsqarostavi, and the monastery of the Baretelni, and to their sites,
and there too they gave offerings and received grace from those holy churches and from the blessed fathers, the worthy and holy ascetics.
They also assigned the boundaries of all those monasteries.
When they departed, they took the blessed Gregory with them. And the ruler Adarnase gave him his son Gurgen as a godson at baptism,
since David the curopalate, son of Bagrat the curopalate, had also been received from the font by the blessed father Gregory. These were the two rulers:
David the curopalate and Gurgen the curopalate. For this reason, at the time of his death, Gurgen the curopalate left a testament, saying:
"Bury me near the bones of my godfather, at his feet, and lay the bones of those other fathers to rest above me." And they did so.
After Gurgen the curopalate, his son Ashot, the eristav of eristavs, eagerly began the new church of Khandzta and lavished countless offerings on it.
At that time the abbot at Khandzta was father Arsenius, a nobleman by birth.
On his advice the new and beautiful church was begun on that rugged rock,
which they levelled over a long time with great labour and solid masonry. They considered the preparation of that site as great a work as if the church had been built in full.
May Christ bless Amona, the builder perfect in wisdom, and all the helpers through whom the building of that church prospered.
Stone and lime were brought from very far away on men's backs over those difficult roads, and everything was weighed on scales, for the builders were buying it.

At that time that God-serving ruler died. He had built holy churches, donated possessions, and laboured on behalf of the poor. He was buried at Khandzta through the arrangement of Arsenius and of his son Mtskhvedi.
Father Arsenius and the blessed John, the brother of Jibril, who completed the new church, both died while serving as abbots of Khandzta.
May Christ grant them rest! Then Gurgen, Ashot's nephew, the great ruler of many peoples, took the seat of eristav of eristavs by the will of God.
