And he completed that new church of Khandzta, and with him all the rulers and nobles who had been appointed [to the work], and all the people of the faithful. And may the Lord grant unfailing good to them all!
But now let us take up again the rest of the earlier account.
For when the name of the blessed father Gregory became renowned and reached Kartli, his blessed mother heard of her son's glory,
for she was still alive and had reached old age. At that time she rejoiced in spirit and grew strong in body, and she gave thanks to Christ,
who had let her hear the good news of her son: news altogether good, a cause for boasting according to the flesh, and something that made her soul crowned.
For she had him as her only child, and after his birth she knew no man again. Instead she remained steadfast in purity, in prayer and fasting and in the constant fear of God.
Her heart had mourned the separation from her son, but the voice of joy strengthened her, and through this consolation she forgot the grief she had felt for her dead.
At once she set out in a litter, and her servants, both men and women, were with her.
She came to Mother Febronia at Mere. Febronia received her with joy and quickly informed the blessed Gregory by letter.
And that holy man, the spotless son, quickly came before his faithful mother, bowed down to her, and gave her the blessing and peace of Christ.
She came to meet her son with joy, kissed him, and said to him:
"My sweet child, I have seen you, whom I longed for, for by the sight of you all those earlier pains have left me."
And their conversation went on at length, with words of many kinds.

The blessed father Gregory said to her: "Grant me your forgiveness, my mother. It was not by my own will that I separated from you; rather, it pleased the will of God that it should be so, as it has now come about.
Up to now you have lacked nothing in this passing life, either in body or in spirit,
But now your labour is owed [?], both spiritually and bodily, according to the commandment of the Lord, which commands honour for parents. And in Wisdom it is written:
"Son, repay your parents for what they gave you, for without them you would not exist." And again it says:
'Whoever dishonors his father is to be reproached, and whoever angers his mother's heart is cursed by the Lord,'
for 'the blessing of father and mother establishes houses forever, but their curse uproots them completely.'
Paul likewise many times commands everyone to honor their parents. These words, and others like them, we hear from the God-inspired spiritual books for the instruction of the faithful.
And I, by the grace of God, will inherit your blessing, as a child who loves his parent, through obedience as far as I am able, according to the will of your heart."
And that blessed man of God comforted her greatly and much edified that most blessed old woman.
She first blessed God and then her son. She entrusted to him the members of her household who had come with her, and said:
"Child, these are entrusted [?] to you as I am, for they have zealously taken upon themselves the service of me." And the holy man said to her: "The apostle says:
'If anyone does not provide for his own, and especially for his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.'
"And it is my duty, mother, to obey your command and to take care of all these concerns of yours." And he arranged everything well, as was proper.
Then the blessed mother Febronia said to that faithful old woman:
"God-loving mother, along with your son, my brother Gregory, I am now your child too.
You will lack no service from us at all, for I see you as Anna the prophetess, who did not leave the temple of the Lord day and night, with prayer and fasting.
So you too always stand firm in the commandments of God, and the goodness of a tree is known by its fruit."
And she joyfully gave thanks to Christ and to those saints.
Then the blessed Gregory arranged, as was fitting, the way of life of his mother and of those who were with her.
He gave a certain serving woman of his mother's in marriage to a husband, and from her was born Basil, the father [abbot] of Khandzta,
who governed Khandzta well as its superior for many years, until his death and his going before the Lord.
But after a long time the blessed mother of father Gregory died at Mere and went to the Lord, for whom she had longed.
The blessed Gregory laid her to rest and gave glory to God, who had granted him to serve his mother well, and he received a full blessing.
But Theodore and Christopher, those blessed great fathers, when they saw that Arsenius and Ephrem, those worthy of God, had grown into young men, mature in wisdom and in stature,
took heart regarding the oath to father Gregory, to whom they had promised not to leave the boys until they had grown up.
Then they left Khandzta secretly by night, taking some brothers with them, and went back to the regions of Kartli,
for the Lord was invisibly calling them by his command, and through them he was building the holy monasteries of Nedzvi and Saint Cyricus.
And it was made known to the blessed Gregory by the Lord that he should no longer hold them back from their zeal,
but should become a helper in that good work. Father Gregory searched for them, found them in Samtskhe, and reproached them for leaving in secret.
But they fell down before him and said: "Forgive us, holy father, for this is the reason we left Khandzta:
so that some fruit might come to be our portion through building new monasteries." And the saint said to them:
"This intention of yours is good, by the will of God; but make me a partner with you in this zeal, for I am not one to spoil what is good."
And they went together into the deserts of the regions of Samtskhe and Kartli, found two places for monasteries, and built cells in both places.
They named Theodore's monastery Nedzvi and Christopher's Saint Cyricus, and they left disciples there.
And all three of these blessed men, Gregory, Theodore and Christopher, came to Khandzta to divide the brothers as was fitting. And when they reached that community,
which was pleasing to God, and greeted them, the blessed Gregory began to speak to the brothers: "People of Christ, listen to me!
At first we came together to this holy desert, these four: I, the poor Gregory, and Laban, bishop of Ishkhani, and Theodore and Christopher.
And for many years these great fathers, pleasing to Christ, were obedient to me as disciples, until the time of God's calling.
And when Christ willed it, Saba became bishop over Ishkhani, and he took brothers away from here.
But now Christ is building those two very fine monasteries in Kartli through Theodore and Christopher.
And just as parents in the flesh divide their property among their children, so Khandzta is the spiritual parent of us all.
Although we had the habit of monks before we came, we have received every blessing here.
And now, by my hand, Khandzta grants brothers to these, its children, so that in their new building work they may be free of care, with the support of well-tested monks,
and so that the spiritual love between the monasteries we have built may remain firm."
And when he had finished these words, he ordered all the brothers to be gathered.
And with the counsel of Theodore and Christopher he chose thirteen brothers from among them to remain at Khandzta as elders,
and he divided all the others equally into three groups, for those assigned to Shatberdi had already been sent to Shatberdi earlier. And he ordered them to be divided by lot, as had been agreed.
Theodore and Christopher rejoiced, but there was a small dispute between them, because Ephrem and Arsenius were in Gregory's portion. He granted Ephrem to Theodore,
and kept Arsenius for himself, and he gave Christopher another brother equal to him, and they were satisfied and rejoiced.
And this was a marvel about those blessed flocks: they did not quarrel with those good shepherds, as though arguing over the place
that would suit any one of them, for they counted themselves as the sheep of those who were always with Christ and were chosen by Christ.
Such was the obedience of those men clothed in victory. And those blessed fathers of ours led the brothers and went back to Nedzvi and to Kvirike-Tsmida (Saint Cyricus),
and Father Gregory helped them with all his heart in their new building work. They blessed the sites of the holy churches and laid the foundations.
As blessed Gregory was setting out, all the brothers said to him, weeping:
"O holy one of God, the word of the Lord is now being fulfilled upon us: 'You will long to see your teacher and will not see him!'
O the tyranny of your holiness! But let your will be done, and not ours.
Holy one, although you are parting from us in this passing world, do not wish to be parted from us for eternity, and may you remember us always in your holy prayers, chosen one of God."
And that blessed man blessed them all with tears and comforted their hearts. He commended them to Christ and to those blessed fathers, and made the sign of the cross over those holy monasteries.
And as he left, Father Theodore and Father Christopher went along the road with him, and they kissed one another with tears.
And they stayed in their own monasteries, while our blessed father came to Khandzta.

In this way I have briefly recorded the lives of those three saints, Theodore, Christopher, and Saba of Ishkhani, because to write out all their deeds fully and truthfully would have made this far too long.
When Khandzta had become renowned through grace and joyful through its spiritual children, at that time the great desert-dweller Father Michael came to Khandzta from Midznadzori,
who had settled at Parekhi, for he was a friend of our blessed father Gregory.
He sought solitude, and found a dwelling place for himself, the caves (Parekhi) of Berta. On this saint's advice he settled in them and advanced well in the virtues of the Lord.
But the enemy, the devil, grieved greatly, because he saw that as holy men multiplied, his own time was being cut short.
He worked great terrors [?] against Michael, openly and in secret, so that he might drive him out of the desert.
But Michael endured with great strength the blows of that sleepless assailant, and with the help of Christ and the intercession of all the saints he put to shame the devil's many kinds of schemes.
Once, Father Michael was some distance from his cell, standing on a high rock, and was a little off his guard [?]. Beliar grew bold against him and threw him down from that height.
But Christ God, the King of all, kept him completely unharmed. Even so, Father Michael became troubled, beset [?] by that unending warfare,
and he sent his disciple to his spiritual teacher, Father Gregory, and told him about all that trial from the evil spirits.
The saint quickly came to help his brother by the power of the Lord. He strengthened him in spirit, and with his own hands he newly made seals of Christ that give victory:
two wooden crosses, for Michael's protection and to drive away the enemies. He set them up on either side, at some distance from his cell, and marked them out as a boundary for that holy man, saying:
"Between these two crosses of Christ, stay without fear, by the help of the Holy Trinity and the power of the precious Cross.
But if you go beyond them, you will again be tried, worse than before."
They prayed, and the blessed Gregory went away. The blessed Michael found complete rest, because by humility he struck down the proud enemy,
since he did not trust in his own righteous deeds, but, relying on God alone, brought his teacher and spiritual brother Gregory to help him. As it is written:
"A brother helping a brother is like a wall that does not fall"; and in keeping with the word of James the apostle:
"Pray for one another, so that you may be healed, for the prayer of a righteous man is very powerful as a help."
And so, by the grace of God, he prevailed completely over the enemies.

The blessed Michael came from the land of Shavsheti, from the village of Norgiali. He became a monk at Midznadzori, and he lived in the caves (Parekhi) for many years. When he died, he was buried there too.
Now his tomb and that of the glorious father Basil, who lived in the caves (Parekhi) after him, are together in one place, and they grant healing to the people who come to them in faith.
Our blessed father Gregory always lived in the two monasteries he had built, Khandzta and Shatberdi, and he filled the hearts of his disciples with the learning of his teaching.
For he not only spoke wisdom about the divine books in every respect,
but he was also a faultless teacher of the hymnody sung in the holy catholic Church, following the order of the whole year,
and he knew well the order of all the feasts, because whatever he had learned he remembered and never forgot.
He had a rich, flexible voice of beautiful sweetness, and his memory was astonishing.
For there is now at Khandzta the hymnal (Iadgari) for the whole year, written by his own hand through the Holy Spirit, and its words are very fine.
He knew the canonical books of the New Testament by heart, and many books of the Old Testament as well.
And the countless non-canonical sayings of the holy teachers he would recite without a book, with his own tongue, beyond what our nature can do,
for wherever the power of God comes to rest, it accomplishes everything beyond human nature and understanding.
Even to Adam everything was subject before he disregarded the commandment.
And because he kept these commandments without blemish, everything went well for him.
Through this not only were his monasteries made firm, but all the deserts of Klarjeti were watered by the rivers of his wisdom.
Many times those holy fathers, the abbots of the monasteries, would come to him for many reasons, and through his wisdom they found relief in every matter.

Throughout all the days of this blessed man, the holy fathers of the monasteries would celebrate the eve of the fast before him at Khandzta. At the beginning of the fast they would receive from him the rule for the great fasts, and then depart.
Once these blessed men were gathered together before this holy man, and Father Gregory was teaching all of them, except the abbot of Opiza, those good words of the life of the soul.
The father of Opiza was grieved and said to him: "Holy father, why have you passed me over in your spiritual words?"
He replied: "Honoured father, I did not pass you over out of disrespect, but for this reason:
Opiza was built before all these deserts, and I have no authority over Opiza or over its abbot."
But with humility he persuaded the holy man to teach him equally with the other fathers,
for all of them regarded him as one of the holy apostles, a mediator between God and men.
Many times the rulers of that time firmly resolved that this blessed man should become a bishop, and they troubled him with great effort to make him submit.
But he did not want such glory, and he explained it to them clearly, saying:
"The holy churches of the deserts, thrones of God's glory, are not lesser than the holy sees of the world.
Although the priesthood is given to all priests by bishops, yet from the first holy desert fathers we have learned this:

the grace that is given to a person at the time of baptism is the same grace we have seen when the newly made monk receives the habit of monasticism, and likewise at the receiving of the holy [?]work.
There is much other testimony as well. But just as in Israel cities were appointed as places of refuge for manslayers, so too the holy deserts are a refuge for all,
for they protect the innocent from the harms of the world, and they are havens for the wounded, giving them hope by granting repentance and by laying down rules.
It is enough glory for me, twice over, if I, weak as I am, can bear the struggle of these holy deserts as is fitting. In them people have found freedom, as Paul said:
'With the freedom with which Christ has set us free,' and 'Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.'
For power was given to them 'to become children of God,' according to the word of John the Evangelist."
The rulers were edified by such words, and they glorified Christ.
After this the blessed father Gregory saw that the godly community of Shatberdi was flourishing, and that the first holy church had been completed and consecrated.
Then he was filled with joy, because the Lord had granted him this good work as his heart desired, by the grace and intercession of the holy Mother of God,
in whose name that holy monastery had been built, for the everlasting glory of the Mother of God, the helper of the helpless and the protector in all things of those who trust in her and praise her,
now and forever. Her Son, the God of all, glorified her beyond words, above all the creatures under his dominion.
For he has already settled her, united in soul and body, in the kingdom that does not pass away, before the glory of his divinity, since she is the firstborn of all the saints,
the light of Christianity. Through her intercession and that of all the saints the Lord saves us, all who believe in him,
but above all he glorifies his chosen ones, who carry out his holy will, for he says: "Those who glorify me I will glorify."
And: "I will grant them a hundredfold here and now, and make them inherit eternal life." Christ fulfilled this unfailing command for the blessed Gregory.

As an honour of unfading glory he granted him the building of glorious desert monasteries, and while Gregory was still in the flesh, God spread the fear and awe of his holiness over kings and over all the people,
like the power of a sovereign whom no one can resist.

After his departure from the world, God glorified him in heaven with the angels, beyond our understanding, and now on earth he is glorified forever by the mouths of his disciples and of those who praise him.
Now the blessed mother Febronia was troubled, because the faithful priest who had been sent by Father Gregory and appointed as their shepherd had died.
But it was made known to her by God that it would now be better to have another priest as "a shepherd for you."
So she wrote a letter to the blessed Gregory and asked for a worthy priest. Then the holy man said to the holy Matoi:
"Beloved son, until a soldier has entered battle, his prowess is not known among the mass of the army, and he receives no gifts from kings.It is
But once he has shown himself valiant, the strength of his fighting becomes known to everyone, and the king rightly grants him abundant gifts.
"So you too, be obedient to my words: by all means take upon yourself the priesthood at the church of the all-holy Mother of God at Mere, as a soldier of the Lord clothed in victory.
And I trust in Christ that you will fight the good fight." But Matoi fell down before him in tears and said to him humbly:
"Forgive me, father. Your holiness knows that I have never disobeyed your command, but now I am not able to do what you have commanded me."
And the holy man said: "You are able, by the power of the Lord.
Now add perfect obedience to your good virtues. I have marked you with the sign of the cross, by the cross of Christ, so that you may set aside every excuse."
When Matoi saw that his teacher's command could not be disputed,
he obeyed his words against his own will. And so, by the will of God, the blessed and wonder-working Matoi, great and glorious in his deeds, became priest of the convent of women.
For in the forty years of his priesthood at Mere no one heard from him an idle word or a useless reply, the kind that becomes a sin for people, as the Lord says:
"For every idle word that people speak, they will give account of it on the day of judgement."

And not only this, but those who saw him could not bring themselves to indulge in idle amusement, because of his reverent restraint and his holy and blameless way of life, for he became a model of goodness for everyone.
She kept true virginity, not only in body but also in soul and word, in hearing and in sight. For that blessed one said:
"Monastic life is called restraint." Because of this the God-loving woman Temestia, deaconess of Meri, said:
"In my forty years as deaconess, and serving at the liturgy all the time, he never once took the censer from my hand."
But he grew weak from his excessive labours, for unceasing prayer, constant thirst and hunger, sleeplessness,
standing upright and frequent kneeling were the blessed man's practice. He struck down the passions of the flesh and weakened the enemies of the soul.
He never missed the services of the hours, except for some cause or illness. His clothing was utterly humble, and so was his food.
Once Matoi was in his own dwelling near Mere.
He learned that thieves were coming, and during the day he prepared bread for them. When the thieves arrived at night, he said to them:
"Believe me, my children, the holy Mother of God commands you not to harm me." But the one who had brought them [?] dared to carry off what the holy man had.
And he said: "I am a servant of the holy Mother of God, and may she punish you, you who are carrying that off."
At that very moment the man fell down, struck by the evil enemy. Then his companions fell before the saint in tears and begged him to heal the man.
He made the sign of the cross over him and said: "The holy Mother of God heals you." And at once the man was restored to health.
And the saint said to him: "Wretched man, why did you lead these men to do evil to me?"
And he gave them hospitality and sent them away in peace. The saint performed many such miracles, and he reached old age.
Illness also came upon him from those heavy labours, and he could not take care of himself. Then the blessed Matoi said:
"This has become a means of downfall [?] for me, that women should serve me, even though these sisters act according to God's will,
it is not proper for a monk to be served by the hands of women. But I have a way to free myself."
There were certain relatives of Matoi among the servants of the mother of Father Gregory at Berta [?], good monks who were his friends.
He sent word to them, and they came joyfully to carry him away on a litter, for he was very weak from his great ascetic struggle.
But all the sisters were filled with tears of mourning, for they were being left orphans of their spiritual father and teacher.
And he blessed them all, full of tears. He made the sign of the cross over them, bade them farewell in peace, and said to them:
"May Christ protect you, by the grace of the Virgin who bore him and of all the saints. And pray for me always."
And he gave a sign to the brothers, and they lifted him on the litter. When they had gone a short way, he ordered them to stop and said:
"Lord, by your word you made the bodies of the weak into living bodies. Give strength to me too, your weak servant."
And at once he became completely strong again, and he went to Berta on his own feet.
He lived through the days of one whole year in full health. Then he departed from this troubled world and went to the world of the living,
as a brave and valiant fighter for Christ, fully clothed in victory, before God with joy. He intercedes for us forever.
At the time of the father's death, the blessed women in Mere saw a vision: Themestia the dean, and Anatole, who was called Antonios, the recluse. Both of them saw it at the same moment, at midnight.
The one who lived in solitude went to the church before the hour when the bell was rung. In the same way the dean also came to the porch of the church, and they greeted each other.
And the archpriest said to him, "Why have you come? Tell me, what did you see?" And he said to him:
"I saw something like your vision, for our blesser Matoi has now died."
And she told her everything: "A man came, splendidly adorned, and said to me:
'The great Matoi is passing over to God. Follow me, so that you may be found worthy to see his glorious passing from this world to the kingdom of heaven.'
"I followed him. He led me to a hill near Berta and said to me: 'Look at Berta and see a glorious vision.'
And I saw a pillar of light coming down from heaven onto that monastery, and a multitude of holy angels descending with the pillar.
Among them was one who looked like a deacon, wearing a stole. They were singing to God with radiant voices. Then I saw the assembly of holy angels again,
in the same form, going up to heaven. In their midst those bodiless beings adorned with light were leading the holy Matoi up by the hand, with indescribable glory and with singing in the highest.
This is my vision about the saint."
The other said to her: "Your vision is truly to be believed. But now hear mine. In his youth the blessed Matoi was tall and handsome,
but now I saw him even more adorned with glory. He was clothed in liturgical vestments of unimaginable radiance,
and in his hands he held golden censers. I was amazed at the vision and said to him: 'How have you become strong after your weakness, teacher?'
"He said to me: 'I served the altar from my youth. Now I have passed from this altar to serve it without end,
for I have been made worthy to stand before the heavenly altar and to serve forever.'"
After they had seen these things, some people came from Berta and told them that Matoi had died at that very hour. And they gave thanks to Christ the wonderworker.
Many other disciples of the blessed Gregory had reached the highest degree of monastic life,
for at times their bodies were seen clothed in the radiance of the holy angels, even more than Matoi's.
Great miracles were done through them, both while they lived in the body and after their death.
But let me speak about the faithful son clothed in Christ whose name was Demetrius.
For he had been raised by the blessed mother Febronia and had become a disciple of father Gregory, and he was counted among Gregory's first disciples.
Many times a man of God saw a pillar of light over him at night, during every prayer of that worthy man, for the Holy Spirit always rested upon him.
He set out for Jerusalem. When he reached Emesa he fell slightly ill, and he perceived through the Spirit that God was calling him. He wrote a letter with his own hand, as follows:
"Chosen ones of Christ, dwelling places of holiness, father Gregory and mother Febronia, my spiritual parents,
you raised me on the food of spiritual teaching instead of milk, and you sent me out on this good road with the provisions of divine learning.
Now my voice falls silent toward you until the Lord comes in glory. For I have reached Emesa, and there I have fallen asleep until the second coming of Christ.
When you count your disciples, look for your son there, and always remember me in your holy prayers, saints of God."
And in that same hour he died, and he was buried there in Emesa.
But the worthy Arsenius and Ephrem, who were mentioned earlier and deserve to be remembered always, disciples and pupils of Gregory —
let us remember them. The will of God was pleased to make them chief shepherds over their own flocks of reasoning beings.
For the great Ephrem became bishop of the see of Atsquri in Samtskhe many years before Arsenius. Afterwards the great Arsenius, in the catholic church
at Mtskheta, the resting place of Christ's tunic, became Catholicos of Kartli. There was love between the two of them because they had been raised together.
But the bishops of Kartli were deeply aggrieved with Mirean, Arsenius's father, for the following reason:
without consulting them, he had forcibly installed his son as catholicos with the help of the people of Samtskhe, with the support and blessing of only a few bishops.
So, as a small reproof and by the Lord's permission, those bishops were stirred up, so much so that even the blessed Ephrem joined in the dispute [?], for their argument was just.
At that time the ruler was the great Mampali Guaram, who was ill-disposed toward Mirean, and he promptly ordered the bishops and the fathers of the desert to assemble.

They all gathered in Javakheti. But father Gregory was not there, nor were all the abbots of the desert monasteries of Klarjeti. For the blessed Gregory was archimandrite, and everyone was eagerly waiting for him.
The leaders of church order argued among themselves about Catholicos Arsenius, but they could not reach a firm decision.
Then the bishop of Erusheti at that time said to everyone:
"When the star of the deserts comes, then everyone's business and plans will be set right." And they said to him:
"Whom do you mean with such confident words?" He said: "Archimandrite Gregory, the builder of Khandzta and Shatberdi."
Then one of the bishops said mockingly among those assembled: "Is he the only shining star?"
But all the others said: "He speaks the truth, for Gregory enlightens others with the light of his teaching and is adorned with the Holy Spirit."
Immediately they saw the saint coming with an escort into the midst of the assembly of the fathers, and his appearance was wonderful.
For the humble garment the old man wore looked like a garment of brilliant, unfading light.
And the cowl on his head looked like a royal crown adorned with precious stones and priceless pearls.
When they saw his divine glory, all went out to meet him with joy, and they gladly followed his words.
At that time Bishop Ephrem arrived. First he greeted his teacher, Father Gregory, and then his brothers the bishops.
Then the blessed Gregory secretly called the blessed Ephrem to him and said to him:
"My son, I adjure you by that honour of the holy high priesthood which you hold: do not oppose your spiritual brother Arsenius." But Ephrem said to him:
"Holy father, my brothers the bishops cannot argue for what is right, and forgive me too,
for from now on I am not Arsenius's sheep, and he is not my shepherd." Then the holy man said to him sternly:
"If you do this, Ephrem, then disown me, as though I were not your teacher."
At these words of his spiritual father and teacher, the blessed Ephrem wept and said to him:
"This command is harsh, sharper than a sword. Now let your will be done and not mine, saint of God." And he said to him:
"Blessed Ephrem, may Christ grant you whatever you ask of him, you who are innocent in heart and upright in mind, made like your teacher Christ, as David says:
'For the Lord our God is upright, and there is no falsehood in him.'"
You know, by your spirit that sees God, how God ordained the catholicate for Arsenius because of his perfection.
But Mirean, his father, brought it into disrepute by rushing it before its time, just as Adam ate the fruit that was not yet ripe.
Now do well to obey me, for the anger of man does not bring about the righteousness of God. And let this guilt of Arsenius be upon me."
After this, when Guaram the sovereign heard that the blessed men had come, he went out to meet them with joy and greeted them humbly.
And when they had sat down, Guaram ordered all the monks to be gathered, and they came. Then he said to them:
"Holy fathers, bishops and desert-dwellers, you all know the canon of the law: it does not allow a bishop or a catholicos to be installed by force."
In this speech he multiplied words of reproach, and he waited for an answer from them.
But everyone's eyes were on Father Gregory and Bishop Ephrem, and for a time they kept silent.
Then the bishops said to Ephrem, "Give the answer: what is right?" And he said:
"Where Father Gregory is present, I do not dare to speak." Then the ruler said to the blessed Gregory:

"Father, everyone is waiting for you to speak the truth, for you are the eldest of all, both in days and in virtues according to the will of God, and it is fitting that the speaking should begin with you."
And he said: "It would have been proper for the high priests to speak first. But now, at your word, I say this:
You true flocks of Christ, listen to this poor old man: Arsenius the catholicos is catholicos by the will of God.
And let those who speak evil of him and do not repent be put to shame and utterly disgraced, in this world and in the age to come."
Although that ruler was wise and devout, he was greatly disturbed by the just rebuke of that righteous man.
For his will overcame his wisdom, and envy did not spare the honor due [to the man], since the venom of the heart is known from the lips. Without thinking, he let out words like these:

"For a long time I had not seen Father Gregory, but I had heard that his wisdom, which even the wise could not grasp, had been changed by old age. What I first heard, I have now seen with my own eyes."
He also said many things about the law, for he was not like ordinary laymen: he was very skilled in speech.
But the blessed Father Gregory said to him: "O ruler, why are you angered by the truth?
Know this: at the councils of the holy fathers of old, the first believing kings were present together with the bishops and the superiors of the monastic order.
They did not presume to teach the law along with them. Instead they asked about the fathers' examination of the law and requested that the word be explained,
for they were zealous for the commandments of God and were witnesses to what the fathers said.
In the canon laid down by the holy apostles and the venerable high priests, it is nowhere ordained that a layman
should presume to take on the teaching that belongs to the bishops and to the fathers who are superiors of the order, or should introduce innovation,
even if it seems right. That is contempt for the law and for the high priests. As for me, according to what you say, Guaram,
I am now changed in nature. But when justice judges you, then you will see yourself brought to understanding, and you will no longer reproach my words."
But the ruler was shaken in mind and said to the bishops, "It is for you to manage your own affairs. Now speak!" And they said to him:
"Guaram, servant of God, a sign from Christ has made us speechless, for today we have seen a glory beyond understanding upon Gregory."
They told him the whole vision they had seen when Gregory came in.
Then terror struck the ruler, for he was humble and God-fearing. Overcome by humility, he fell down before the blessed Gregory and said to him:
"Holy one of God, forgive me, for I have offended you." Gregory said to him: "May Christ forgive you all your faults."
Then Guaram, the great ruler, entertained everyone well. During the meal, when Guaram had grown merry with wine, the bishops said with one voice:

"This rebuke concerning Arsenius was indeed fitting. But from now on, let Arsenius be catholicos of all Kartli and spiritual father of all, and let the former suspicion among everyone be completely dissolved,
so that we may carry out the dignity of our Christian calling in peace and quiet, and may find a good defense before the thrones of Christ."
Guaram the ruler and all the people said: "Amen, so be it!"
Then the ruler asked the bishops: "Holy ones of God, suppose a layman of our land,
learned in the divine books and trained in languages as well, goes to Jerusalem or to other holy places and sees some good practice

that is fitting for Christianity but does not exist among us. Or suppose he comes to understand something from the holy books and, on his own authority, teaches it to the uninstructed people. Is that good or not?"
In saying this, he meant it to be heard by certain talkative people.
But they said: "It is written: 'The appointed load is enough for a ship. If you make it heavier, it will sink; and if it is too light, the winds and waves will carry it away.'
In the same way, the load of the law and the order of Christianity that our land now holds is very good, and God is pleased with it.
And so we stand as guarantors: if anyone holds to it firmly, practises it in deed without changing it, and does not trade in mere words,
'he will receive a hundredfold here and now and will inherit eternal life,' according to the word of the Lord. And we have accepted the earlier word that Father Gregory spoke.
And we say this: if a layman, as you have commanded, comes to understand some new good rule,
silence is better, as the apostle James said: 'Not many of you should be teachers, brothers.'
And if he cannot keep silent, he should not preach on his own authority. Instead he should inform his own bishop, and if it is fitting, the bishop should teach it to his flock.
But if that layman pushes ahead out of insolence and imposes a new and different rule on the people, such a person,
instead of gaining anything, will be condemned along with the quarrelers and opponents at the glorious coming of the Lord."
And the ruler said: "Truly this spiritual council of divine providence is just. And if the reader of a book needs to read it,
how much more must the one who teaches rule and law read it, and keep a careful watch over himself in every way, as it says: 'Physician, heal yourself first!'"
And those laymen were ashamed at that rebuke of the ignorant for laying down rules, and they were forgiven by the leaders of the law.
And when they had finished the meal, they took their leave of the great prince, and he sent them all away with joy.
At that time they brought the good news to Arsenius, since he was not at that council:
"After God, your teacher Father Gregory has confirmed you as catholicos." And he joyfully gave thanks to Christ and to the holy man.
And Bishop Ephrem, following Father Gregory's command, renewed his love for Catholicos Arsenius as it had been before,
for he quickly calmed a quarrel that would otherwise have taken a long time to settle. This quarrel was between the catholicos and the bishops, and above all the ruler Guaram.
And these blessed men, Catholicos Arsenius and Bishop Ephrem, used to come to visit their teacher, Father Gregory.
And Catholicos Arsenius consecrated the old church of Khandzta and spread joy to all the churches of Kartli, for he adorned the patriarchal throne completely, and it was adorned with grace.
And when Father Gregory died, Arsenius was present at his burial.
Arsenius served as catholicos for twenty-seven years. Then he departed from this world and with gladness came into the presence of Christ, and he has grace to help us.
And the great Ephrem brought about much good for our land. Formerly, the catholicoi of the East used to bring the holy chrism from Jerusalem.
But Ephrem, by Christ's command, established the consecration of the chrism in Kartli, by the decree and with the joyful testimony of the patriarch of Jerusalem.
And Kartli is reckoned to be the wide land in which the liturgy is offered and all prayer is performed in the Georgian language.
But the Kyrie eleison is said in Greek; in Georgian it means "Lord, have mercy," or "Lord, have mercy on us."

This blessed Ephrem served as bishop for forty years, adorned by the Holy Spirit. He exposed people's hidden deeds as though they were in plain view, and with a word he healed sick people who had been given up for dead,
but with a word, too, he put the disobedient to death. He also performed many other miracles.
He died at a good old age, full of grace, and came with joy before Christ, and he is an intercessor for us believers forever.
Such were the God-clothed disciples of Father Gregory.
The great Epiphanius, through his humility, reached the measure of his teacher. By shedding tears he drove out evil spirits, he quickly healed the sick, and he performed many other miracles,
correcting the disobedient with blows and saving the faithful from death by prayer.
Once, in the summertime, he and the brothers with him were coming down from the mountains of Khorasun. They saw a suitable spot and sat down to eat bread.
Along that same road came a certain woman, and she had her son with her, a boy of seven. The boy was handsome to look at and quick of mind.
As they came into sight of the blessed father Epiphanius, the pangs of death seized the boy, and because of that convulsive illness his soul was hurrying to leave his body.
His mother, wailing bitterly, snatched up her son, ran to the saint, and cried out pitifully like this:
"O holy man of God, help me, for I have no other help! This son of mine is dying on me, and after God I have fled to you."
She laid her son down at the feet of Epiphanius. He rose, full of tears, for he was compassionate by nature, fell down before Christ, and said:
"O Lord our God, Jesus Christ, look on my tears and on the tears of this pitiable woman. Have mercy on this boy and command his soul to dwell
in its own body for many years, to console this poor woman and to glorify you, the only Son, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, unto the ages. Amen."
He made the sign of the cross, took the boy's hand, and said to him: "The Lord Jesus Christ heals you. Arise, child, and live!"
At once the pain and weakness left his body, and all distress left his soul.
He got up cheerful. The saint gave him to his mother and ordered that he be given food, and the woman joyfully offered thanks to God and to the saint.
She and her son went on their way together in peace. The boy lived well into old age and glorified God.
Again, certain other believing people had a young boy who had been harmed by the enemy from birth: he was deaf and mute and lacking in mind.
But to look at his body, he seemed healthy, and he grew like any other boy.
When he was ten years old, Father Epiphanius was already being spoken of as a worker of miracles, and he came to the village where the afflicted boy lived.
The boy's mother took him out to the road along which Father Epiphanius was traveling.
When she saw him, she begged him for her son's sake with bitter tears and firm faith. The blessed man wept and sighed, and cried out with a contrite heart:
"Christ God, who out of love for mankind became man and suffered in order to heal those who suffer, now, merciful Lord,
Why is this sinless creature of yours tormented by the devil, to expose our sins?
"You, God of countless mercy, have pity on him, free him from all afflictions, and give joy to his parents."
He made the sign of the cross over the child and gave him back to his mother healed. At once the mute boy began to speak with understanding, and the deaf boy could hear well,
when the evil demon was driven out of him by the prayer of that blessed man. Those who saw this wonder glorified God.
Then the woman brought her husband, and they brought two cows to Epiphanius as an offering,
but he gave the cows to the child who had been healed and blessed them. They went away with joy and gave thanks to God.
This same blessed Epiphanius once went before the great Abul-Asad at harvest time to ask for provisions [rochiki] for Khandzta.
Abul-Asad said to him: "Whatever your brothers reap in one day, I give to you."
Abul-Asad gave the same instructions to his wife, who was at Gunatle, and he himself went away to another land.
Epiphanius gathered his brothers, who were good reapers, and they came to Gunatle as had been agreed earlier.
They began to reap in the good field with great zeal, until the middle of that day.
But some wicked men told their lady that the brothers would reap all of that very fine wheat before evening.
She was troubled and sent a man to tell them to stop reaping. Epiphanius was some way off from the brothers, and they did not listen to the man she had sent.
In anger she sent other men, who drove them out of the field by force.
Then Father Epiphanius was displeased with the brothers for not listening to the man who had been sent first,
for he was truly a servant of Christ and did not want to see strife. So he said:
"Lord, forgive your handmaid this insult to us, and care for her better by sending her small trials, so that she may learn not to scorn the poor."
At that very moment an evil spirit struck her down, because the spirit of grace had left her on account of her insolence.
Epiphanius was told at once. He went to her with his brothers, and they prayed for her with all their hearts.
She was in a very pitiable state, and she was quickly healed, because the spirit of grace came back to dwell with her as her guardian forever, and she was harmed no more.
From then on she changed for the good. She bowed down before the brothers, and she sent them away with joy and with great gifts.
For Christ adorned Father Gregory with miracles and humility, and his disciples in the same way, according to the word of the Apostle:
"Let your humility be manifest." For this reason the surpassing humility of Epiphanius was plainly seen, as follows.
Once, at a certain time, some good monks, brothers, had come from Nedzvi, and blessed Father Gregory said to them in private conversation:
"Is there perfect humility among the brothers in your monastery, in deed and not just in word?" And they said to him:
"There is, through your prayers, as you yourself know." And at the very moment they said this, the bell was struck for the liturgy.
And when blessed Gregory began the service, the archdeacon asked aloud who would celebrate, and Gregory ordered Epiphanius to celebrate the liturgy, for he had appointed him superior of Khandzta.
And Epiphanius put on his vestments to celebrate the liturgy, and other priests with him, for that day was Sunday.
And when they had gone up to the altar and Epiphanius began to say the "Holy God" before the exclamation, Father Gregory went up to the altar, struck him on the head with his staff and said to him:
"Be silent." And he fell silent without being troubled. And Gregory ordered him to go to the diaconicon and take off his vestments.
Then all the people were filled with astonishment and dread. But he went and took off his vestments, then came back and stood before his teacher for a long time.
And Gregory again ordered him to vest and celebrate the liturgy. And he vested with joy and fell down before blessed Gregory, and Gregory made the sign of the cross over him.
And he went up to the altar, victorious over the sickness of pride, and began to offer those bloodless sacrifices.
But no one dared to ask the holy man the reason for this act, until he himself told those brothers from Nedzvi.
"Did you see, beloved brothers, the humility of Epiphanius, made perfect in deed? Believe me, I speak the truth before God:
he has committed no fault. Because of his fear of God, his holiness and his humility, the grace of the Holy Spirit has always rested upon him.
There is also the humility of one who has been humbled by his faults. But what comparison is there between light and darkness?
For many among these brothers, adorned with faithful humility, are clothed in the garment of true light.
And I did this so that you would see it, because you spoke of the perfect godly humility of your brothers."
And they fell down before him and said, "Although the brothers of our monastery are good in their virtues, they are not capable of this humility."

And when the venerable Epiphanius had celebrated the liturgy, all received communion of the holy mystery, the body and blood of Christ, and together gave thanks to the Holy Trinity, the Creator of all.
Among the fathers of Shatberdi there were very many, one after another, who were outstanding for the courage of their monastic life, and some who shone with the grace of prophecy,
just as the other deserts shone from time to time with holy men. Among them, in our own times, the great Jacob shone in the gorge of Midznadzori,
like the morning star among the stars, adorned beyond what our words can tell with grace of many kinds, together with his godly companions.
But so as not to lengthen this book, I have passed over all of them and come to the miracles of our blessed father Gregory, which I learned from trustworthy men.
But I could not write down everything, because of my ignorance. For I expected that this Life would be written by the wise and perfect fathers who lived in our times:
the great Sophronius, a blessed father, who renovated and rebuilt the church of Shatberdi (may his crown be forever), and the God-clad father Hilarion of Parekhi,
and the worthy hierarchs of Christ, Giorgi, bishop of Mats'kveri, and Stephen, the first bishop of Tbeti, and others like them. And as those blessed ones [?]
For once, when the blessed Gregory was in his own dwelling cell, no fire was ever kindled in that cell, nor was a lamp lit, nor in those of the other brothers.
And at the hour of dawn the dean said to the sacristan: "Go to the father and listen whether he is asleep or awake."
And when he went, he saw a great brightness coming out from inside that cell.
He came running back quickly and cried out: "A fire has broken out in the father's cell!"
The dean said to him: "Be quiet, son, and do not be afraid!
It is not a consuming fire, but the illuminating Spirit of God." For the dean had many times seen that glorious vision.
And he went to the cell and looked through a crack in the wall and saw the saint with his hands outstretched, and from his body came forth rays of light in the shape of a cross.
And he was adorned with glory and shone like the sun.
And the dean joyfully gave thanks to Christ, and for a long time he held back the ringing of the bell for the hour, until that vision had changed.
And again, once in wintertime, the brothers were bringing timber down in the forest of Khandzta. And the blessed Gregory was with them, standing in a place where he could be seen.
And a certain old brother was crossing a difficult spot on the path down which the logs were sent, and the other brothers, not knowing this, let loose a very large log.
And when the brother saw the log coming at him with great force, he was afraid, and he had no way to escape it. He cried out in a loud voice:
"Father, help me!" And he made the sign of the cross over the log and said, "In the name of Christ, stop, log!"
And his word, like an immovable rock, stopped it in that rough, icy place where it was rushing down terrifyingly, and he told the brother to cross with confidence.
And when the brothers saw this miracle, they were amazed and glorified God.
After this, the blessed one was once near Shatberdi, and a woman came to him in faith,
who held in her arms her little son, about two years old, whose hands and feet had been drawn up and contracted by the enemy, and whose face was twisted round backward.
She came with many tears and laid her son down before the feet of the saint and spoke to him thus:
"Holy one of God, have mercy on this child whom men have given up on, for after God it is to you that I flee."
And when the saint saw her great lamentation, he took pity on her, and his tears began to flow, and they became a furnace for the assailant,
for, unseen by men, Gregory's prayers were burning that mighty and wicked demon and driving him out.
Then he said: "The name of Christ drives you out, devil; depart forever from this innocent infant."
And he made the sign of the cross. And at that very moment the evil spirit fled, and the child was completely healed.
And his mother joyfully gave thanks to God and to the saint. And they went home rejoicing, and the child lived on in good and complete health.
And again, there was another woman who had been afflicted with a flow of blood for a long time.
He heard of this miracle and went eagerly to the saint, but he could not bring himself to make his own illness known [?],
so in silence, sighing, he drenched the saint's feet with tears and begged to be healed.
The brothers withdrew a little at a sign from the saint, for he had perceived the hidden affliction in spirit. He held out his right hand so that the man might touch it.
The man did so. At that very hour he was healed of his infirmity, and he went home with joy, glorifying God.
For the goodness and virtue of the blessed father Gregory are full of wonders.
Near Shatberdi there was a certain man of common rank. He had a wife and children and a great deal of property.
They lived their life in joy, for they were people of sound faith.
For her greater good, an infirmity came upon the woman, so that Christ might heal her by the hand of that righteous man and expose the shameful assailant to disgrace.
By his devices, the assailant had pressed all ten fingers of her hands down against her palms, and he tormented her severely with a terrible racking pain.
At that time a divine insight made her aware of the holiness of the blessed father Gregory. The woman quickly took one of her sons with her and came before the blessed man.
By the will of God, the saint was then at one of the estates belonging to Shatberdi.
With many tears and lamentations, she began to beg him for help with the infirmity that had come upon her.
When he saw her faith and her tears, he had great pity on her.
He then ordered one of the priests to go to the church and bring a blessing: oil from the lamp that burned without ceasing before the icon of the holy Mother of God.
He himself stood with his hands outstretched to pray before God, with unceasing sighs and tears flowing like a spring, until the priest came back.

When the priest had brought the oil from the lamp, Gregory called the woman, made the sign of the cross over her hands, and anointed them with the oil in the form of a cross in the name of the Holy Trinity and through the intercession of the holy Mother of God. He said:
"May your hands be healed." At that very moment all her fingers straightened, and no trace of the affliction was left in her at all,
for the harmful demon fled in terror from the prayers of the blessed Gregory.
So she went home in joy, glorifying Christ God.
Later the woman brought her husband and her children, and she presented a large offering to the saint.
They all received a blessing and went away joyful, proclaiming the miracle among many people.
In the time of this saint, the ruler Ashot the Kouropalates conquered many lands. He built the fortress of Artanuji as a residence for the queen, his wife.
He lived well in that fortress for many years.
But the Enemy led that ruler astray. He brought a harlot into the fortress and committed adultery with her,
for the demon of lust inflamed him greatly. He had never had such a habit before, but he was overcome by that evil sin.
When the blessed Gregory heard of this soul-corrupting affair, he was greatly distressed.
He told the holy Gregory, that great old man who dwelt in the churches, for he was a worker of miracles and greatly honoured by God and by men.
On his advice, he rebuked the ruler to his face. The ruler promised to give up that sin and to send the woman away, since he had been the one who brought her there.
But he could not keep his own command, because he was enslaved to desire.
The blessed Gregory found a suitable time, when the curopalates was far from Artanuji. One day he set out from Shatberdi and arrived at evening at the foot of that fortress.
He sent a man to the woman to ask for food and let her know his reason for stopping there.
She rejoiced with great joy and sent many kinds of provisions for the saint and his disciples.
When day dawned, he sent a man to her again, asking her to come and see him.
Then, rejoicing even more, she came quickly to the saint with two of her maidservants, hoping to be found worthy of that blessed man's sign of the cross.
But he did not make the sign of the cross over her. Instead, he ordered her to sit apart.
At a sign from their teacher the disciples drew aside, and so did the serving women, for fear of the saint had spread over everyone.
Then the blessed Gregory said to her: "O wretched woman! Why have you thrust yourself between husband and wife, to your own eternal perdition, through that evil sin
by which you are enslaved to the devil? And why, for some worthless reason, have you become a snare for a great ruler?"
And he said with tears, "Saint of God, I am not my own master, since the curopalates has very great love for me. And now I do not know
what I should do, for the command in your words has greatly shaken me." And the holy man said to him:
"Son, be fully obedient to the words of poor me, and I will stand as your guarantor before Christ, so that he himself may forgive all your sins."
She said to him: "Holy father, I am in your hands. Take care of what is best for my soul."
Only then did he make the sign of the cross over her. He blessed her with prayer, armed her with grace, and gave her a cord from his own sandals to tie around her waist as a belt. And she did so.
The saint said to her: "My child, today the salvation of your soul has come about, for I will bring you to the blessed mother Febronia."
And she rejoiced greatly. The blessed Gregory ordered her maidservants to go on to the fortress, and he said to the woman:
"My child, go on ahead and walk before us."
In this way he brought her to Mere, because the blessed mother had been part of the plan from the beginning. He entrusted the woman to her and said to her:
"Take care of her as is fitting, take care of her, even when the curopalates makes inquiry, for you see that her heart is contrite.
She said: "May Christ take good care of his handmaid, whom he has found through you, venerable father."
These blessed ones talked together alone for a long time.
This was also the custom of the father superiors of that time: they undertook nothing without the advice of mother Febronia.
One of the sisters was walking near them and heard one word, but did not dare to listen to the rest, for holy Gregory said to the blessed Febronia:
"What did the angel say to you?" For God was always among them.
When the curopalates reached the fortress, he asked only for that woman. When he did not find her, he was deeply grieved.
He came to understand everything that had happened, and that it was not through any human snares that the ruler had fallen in love with her,
but that he had been so overcome by the devices of the devil that he forgot his self-restraint. And he quickly came to Mere. But the blessed Febronia hid that woman.
After the curopalates had prayed in the church of the holy Mother of God and received the blessing of Mother Febronia, he began to speak:
"Do you know, mother, why I have come now?" She said to him: "The Lord knows why you have deigned to come here." And he said to her:
"My coming has happened for this reason: there was a woman who was treasurer of our household, and all our possessions were in her hands,
and Father Gregory has brought her here, and we have lost a great deal of our wealth.
Now order her to come to the fortress once and give us an account of everything, and then come back to you again, as she wishes."
But Febronia answered him sharply: "Making excuses, excuses for sins, with men who work iniquity."
When the curopalates heard this, he was ashamed, abashed by her just rebuke, and he stayed silent for a long time, like a man defeated,
for people strong in spirit, armed with divine zeal, had overcome a ruler strong in the flesh. And the grieved curopalates said from the distress of his heart:
"Blessed is the man who is no longer alive!" And he quickly rose and began to leave.
Then the blessed Febronia calmly tried to keep him there so that she might give him hospitality, but he would not stay,
for his own mind accused him. Once the passion of carnal love had left him, he recognized his own fault.
Yet he rejoiced in spirit, because wisdom had driven out that harmful faintheartedness. He praised the mastery of those saints, and still more God, the giver of victory,
and he departed with joy, for with a pure heart he honoured those blessed ones as people who would make his soul crowned forever.
But the Enemy brought a greater passion upon the ruler Adarnase, who was the son of Ashot the curopalates. At the slander of a harlot
with whom he was committing adultery, he unjustly put away his faithful wife on a false charge of fornication and sent her to her own country, Abkhazia, from where he had brought her.
But Christ revealed to his servant Gregory all the injustice
that had been done to that innocent queen. Because of this the blessed Gregory rebuked Adarnase many times,
but that ruler, through vain obstinacy, was overcome by his own wickedness and married another wife.
Then Father Gregory foretold the punishments for those sins that were to come upon him by God's permission.
He said this: "Because you did not listen to the words of me, a poor man, you will be given over to evil diseases, and the sons you now have will be tormented by demons,
"And you will not be healed, neither you nor your sons, until you are forgiven by the queen, that handmaid of God who was unjustly punished;
even if she departs from the body, yet from her tomb she will forgive your sons;
but that harlot, the accuser, Christ will soon expose, more than all who have gone astray, for her shameless boldness and wickedness."
And Adarnerse was greatly afraid at the words of blessed Gregory and fell down before the saint; but he raised him up and said to him:
"May Christ grant you forgiveness of your sins; but know this: what I have said will be fulfilled in its own time, so that all may understand the fruit of disobedience."
And after a few days Adarnerse was struck by a piercing, aching disease, which is called nikrisi (gout).
And he was bitterly tormented by those pains, for until that time he had been entirely unharmed; and at once he sent a good man, whose name was Kupra, before the queen to ask forgiveness.
And when that messenger of Adarnerse arrived at Persati, where her tomb now is, he saw his queen in great monastic life, she who was the daughter of the ruler Bagrat Sharoeli (of Shaori);
for her clothing was a contemptible coarse cloak (chokha), and she wore the holy schema, and a great load of firewood hung on her, and the blessed woman was carrying it to her dwelling;
she whose name at first was Bevreuli and afterwards Anastasia, for she put the devil utterly to shame;
and now the faithful find healing through her grace when they take earth as a blessing (eulogia) from her tomb.
When that man, the messenger, saw this, he recognized her and fell down before her on behalf of Adarnerse and said to her:
"O doer of Christ's will, I beseech you, have mercy on my lord, who has been justly punished by God on account of you, and do not curse him, but forgive him his great sins."
And she said to him: "I swear to you by Christ, never has a curse come forth from my mouth, nor do I curse him.
May Christ forgive him all his sins and heal him in soul and body."
And at once Adarnerse was healed, for that man, the messenger, took note of the hour when she blessed his lord.
And when he returned, he found him entirely unharmed, and he gave thanks to Christ with joy.
But after not many years, when the ruler Adarnerse had sons, Gurgen the curopalates and Sumbat,
they were grievously tormented by the enemy, and at once he sent them to Persati in paupers' clothing and with royal offerings to pray at the tomb of the blessed queen, for she had died.
And when they had prayed, they were completely healed, according to the word of blessed Gregory, and they went to their home with joy, glorifying Christ, the God of all.
But that accusing woman became grievously possessed by a demon and went mad, and other trials also came upon her in accordance with her wicked deeds;
and so terrible and horrifying were the sight of her and the hearing of her words.

And when she came to her senses, then the wretched woman went before Mother Febronia and fell down before her with tears, and confessed all her sins and begged her with lamentation to intercede for her with Father Gregory.
And she wrote him a letter of entreaty, but the blessed one did not listen; instead he wrote back to her:
"Harsher trials were stirred up against her because she became a stumbling block to the God-serving ruler and separated him from his faithful wife,
for she spread his name abroad as that of a fornicator, and moreover she shed the blood of an innocent youth.
Now let her be repaid according to the wickedness of her deeds, even unto death."
But blessed Febronia said: "The judgment of Father Gregory is true, for he did not use force against that holy [?], as the apostle said:
'The spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets.' Rather, as was fitting, he comforted that despairing woman, for he was full of the wisdom of both lives.
And great miracles were seen through him and through some of his disciples.
And now their tombs pour forth healing for those who pray with faith.
And that woman remained in the [?] until her death, for although she was in grievous torments, her mind remained alive.
And when she died, Mother Febronia ordered that she be buried near the sisters who had done the will of Christ, so that those innocent ones might justify the greatly guilty woman before Christ.
But the Lord showed a sign: at the burial of the other dead, she was found three times lying at the inner door of the Akeldama,
and they no longer dared to lift the body of that sinful woman. Only then did they report everything to blessed Febronia,
for she was very old and was not able to go to the burials of those who had fallen asleep. And she said:
"This must be made known to blessed Gregory, for he is the one in charge of this matter." And she wrote him a respectful letter, as follows:
"May the Lord have mercy on us through the holy Cross and through the help of your worthy prayers, Christ-clad Father Gregory,
who always share in the prayer of me, the poor one. You, holy man of God: your assailants prepared snares for you with every kind of wickedness,
like a hunters' trap, and they began to make war on you, who had done no wrong, for they fought you treacherously and unexpectedly, with fierce and cruel visions,
like a troop of horsemen, and at times like a multitude of raging beasts, often appearing in terrifying form.
And so they stirred up against you a storm of struggles, invisible and visible.
But humility adorned with holiness, planted in your person, overcame them all, and your fiery and righteous spirit burned up those harmful enemies, invisible and visible.
"Because of this grace, the power of God is your strength, for you have holiness in the likeness of the holy angels, which is the dowry of victory,
fenced about with constant prayer and fasting and much kneeling, offering holy tears from your sleepless eyes and from your watchful soul,
you, holy priest, who rest among the righteous called into the Church, divine teacher,
strength of the faithful, who rebuke rulers without respect of persons and instruct them with the rod of teaching, because of which your words are fulfilled prophetically among men.
"But now is the time for forgiveness: show mercy to that condemned woman, as befits your holiness,
for the rest of my message will be made known to you by the bearer of this letter. And always help me, here and in the age to come. Amen."
And when the blessed Gregory had read Febronia's letter and understood everything, with tears he gave thanks to Christ and wrote a letter to those sisters who had been laid to rest, in this manner:
"Lovers of Christ, who in the short time of the ways of this world, from your youth until death, have been made victorious for Christ's sake, according to the word of the Apostle:
'For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God; when that life of ours is revealed,'
then you also will be revealed in the glory of the age to come.' You who are called blessed by the wise and are unknown to the ignorant,
who, like good merchants, used this passing world to buy unfailing wealth; who are now asleep in the flesh and awake in the spirit,
counted as dead by the dead and alive forever through Christ, who through that temple of the spirit exchanged earth for heaven,
flowers of virginity, made like the Mother of God, rejoicing before her, waiting for the eternally glorious coming of her Son!
"You who out of weakness have reached unchangeable power, and who after death are fully able to give recompense in two forms, according to people's conduct,
just as we have now seen the just judgment carried out through you. For this I, the poor Gregory, and Mother Febronia are grateful for your help.
And now we beg you on behalf of that pitiable woman: ask Christ to forgive her sins, and count her bones worthy to lie with your bones, and her soul worthy to be with your soul.
And above all, strive at the second coming of the Lord, for you have grace to help the faithful, and you await the endless glory and the inexpressible joy that you are to attain.
But may your intercession always help us, so that we too may be made worthy of that blessed life in the age to come. Amen."
And when they read that letter of the blessed Gregory to those departed sisters, and also announced Mother Febronia's command aloud,
only then did they accept that dead woman in her own original place, where she had been laid three times, and from that day she was moved no more.
For the blessed father Gregory became the cause, first of the exposure of her sins, and afterward of consolation and forgiveness.
And repentance, too, was a great help to the sinful woman before God, who does not desire the death of the sinner
but his turning back and repentance. And those who understood marveled and glorified God.
Christ worked miracles such as these through the hand of the blessed Gregory: the sick,
those gripped by diseases of every kind, and those troubled by unclean spirits were healed through his prayer and tears, as those who begged him in faith asked.
And not only people saw him as a safe harbor, but even the wild animals of the field.
For once this blessed man was in the mountains near Shatberdi on some business, and brothers were also with him,
and a deer came out where they could see it, for hunters had surrounded it and it had no way to escape their hands.

Then it ran toward those monks, passed through them all, and, as though it had understanding, came to the blessed Gregory, laid its head on his holy hands, and seemed to weep over the evil that had come upon it.
But he comforted it and said: "In the name of Christ these enemies of yours will not be able to harm you; do not be afraid."
When those men saw this, they were greatly amazed and glorified God. They came to the holy man and made the sign of the cross.
He blessed them and, in place of the deer, gave them other meat for food, and they went away. He let the deer go in peace.
Likewise, once when he was in his own cell at Khandzta, many hunters surrounded four wild goats near the monastery.
The goats ran into the cell where Father Gregory was sitting and gathered around the holy man.
He understood why they had come, comforted them, and gave orders that the hunters be given hospitality and sent on their way.
He gave the animals food and let them go in peace.
When Father Basil was a young man, he kept watch for Father Gregory.
An evil boil came out on his neck. People call this kind of boil "blessed" (kurtkheuli), but in old times it was called "satali."
And Basil lay stricken with that bitter illness and suffered for only about four days. Then the blessed Gregory asked:
"Where is the young Basil?" The brothers told him about his illness, and he ordered that Basil be called. But they said to him:
"He cannot come." Then he said to them: "Tell him from me: 'Father Gregory commands you.'"
When Basil heard the summons, the command of his teacher gave him strength, and he came before him.
Gregory asked him: "What is wrong with you?" With his hand Basil showed him the boil, which had spread over a large area.
Then blessed Gregory struck hard with his hand on the place where the boil was, and said to Basil:
"You have lost heart for nothing, for there is nothing wrong with you at all."
Basil passed his hand over that place, and not even a trace of the evil boil remained. Those who saw this miracle glorified God.
At that time there were in Jerusalem certain disciples of blessed Gregory. They were fine men, good monks, perfect in wisdom, and workers of miracles.
They sought the Kingdom and fled from the glory of this world. They were worthy priests and sons of great nobles.
They were kinsmen of the great Ephrem, bishop of Matsqveri. They wrote this letter from Jerusalem to Father Gregory, and it had arrived at Khandzta earlier.
I have now copied their letter into this book, all of it and without change. It reads as follows:
"May the Lord grant us the holy prayer of our holy, venerable and great father Gregory, and may He make us sinners worthy of it,
we your poor and unworthy servants, useless Arsenius and feeble Macarius, your spiritual nephew and son, and the nephew and son of all your sons.
Great father, venerable in the Lord, our lord, worthy of God, lord and head of that holy desert, teacher of the Christ-loving people and enlightener of all:
in your holy humility, forgive us for this bold, ignorant and foolish letter written by your poor and unworthy servants.
Trusting in your love of God, we have dared to write this boldly, O you who are renowned at that immortal banquet.
We, who are sinners beyond all other people, humbly greet you and send you the grace and prayer of the Holy Resurrection, and of all those
who are in the holy city of Jerusalem and in the surrounding region, at the holy places where Christ our Lord is worshipped.
"You, holy and venerable father, and all your children: in faith, and in keeping with our longing for all of you, forgive us, and accept the eagerness of our greeting to you!
Likewise, holy father, a man came here from where you are: a servant of God, a Greek priest from this land. He had seen you, father,
and he told us that God is keeping you in peace, and that your venerable life of holiness in that holy desert is in good health.
We unworthy ones were greatly refreshed and rejoiced. With our unworthy mouths, we sinners dared to offer thanks to God, the lover of mankind, for this news and for the joy of hearing of your peace.
"Then that man of God, Moses, came here, also from where you are, and we have given him this letter.
Here he went round all these holy places and venerated them. Together with all the faithful, he prayed for you, father, continually, remembered you, and praised you greatly.
We rejoiced beyond measure, and for our own sake and the sake of our sinful souls we dared to write this letter.
Falling down before you, we entreat your goodness, you who are wholly good, and the sweet lordship of your love of God,
that you will not neglect us, your servants, in your holy prayer, O God-clothed father, great teacher of the saints.
"Just as our soul has entreated your holy worthiness before, so now too we entreat you:
for the love of Christ, remember us in your worthy prayers and before that holy flock of yours, O worthy one of God, venerable father and our lord.
As for how we live in this holy place, Holy Saba, and all our news, that same Moses will report it to you, holy father.
We tell you this trusting in your kindness; may your holiness believe it.
In these holy places we always venture to remember you in our prayers, so that the Lord may make us unworthy ones worthy to have a full share in your holy prayer.
"Father, [?] Euphrosyne, our sister: for the love of God, ask after her, and extend your prayer and blessing to her as well. Amen."
Concerning such worthy men, the early holy fathers said:
"The fathers who will be found doing the will of Christ in the last times will be ahead even of us and of our fathers."
The blessed father Gregory, the wonderworker, governed all the holy desert monasteries of Klarjeti in this way:
he cared well for the faithful monks, brought the guilty to repentance, and drove out completely those who were disobedient to righteousness.
A certain elder of Opiza used to say: "In my youth I was driven out of Opiza three times by father Gregory because of the wickedness of my ways."
But ever since the great monasteries of Klarjeti were built, their priests and deacons have been ordained by the bishops of Ancha, and likewise when they consecrated bishops.
If all those desert monasteries had not given the same testimony, and if the writing of them all had not been a true witness,
the catholicos would not have been willing to lay hands on the candidate of that bishopric to make him bishop, nor would it have been acceptable under the just judgment of the council,
even though the see of Ancha had existed for countless ages before these monasteries were built, and many of its bishops had worked wonders well.
But Christ honored those holy desert monasteries, so that they would have as their head a blameless, holy and worthy bishop,
as befits that holy see, which was kept virgin from the corruption of heresy and perverse teaching, and was built in the name of the holy icon of Christ God.
In the time of the blessed father Gregory, the worthy high priest Zachariah worked these miracles.
For at the monastery of Tbeti, on the steep slope near it, a terrible rock was shifting, and the monks were fleeing their dwellings in fear.
But Zachariah stood firm in hope and said to them: "Tomorrow you will see this rock lying in a place where it will do us no harm."
And so it happened, for the fathers did not notice it moving at all.
And the next day it lay firmly in an unexpected place, the very place the holy man had told them, and they glorified Christ.
Once, at the time of the grape harvest, this same Zachariah was sitting at Tbeti under his ripe climbing vines, which a starling had often been eating.
He made the sign of the cross, and the bird died at once. Then he made the sign of the cross again, and it came back to life and flew off with its companions.
Once a countless swarm of locusts came near the border of Ancha. But the blessed bishop Zachariah sent his staff out to meet them in the hands of priests,
and through the grace of his servant the Lord destroyed that multitude of locusts, which was covering the sky and blocking the sun. And the faithful people glorified God.
Another time two terrible serpents appeared in the vineyard of Ancha, and the vinedressers fled.
But Zachariah killed them by prayer, and those men joyfully gave thanks to Christ.
There were other worthy, wonder-working bishops like him at Ancha as well. Like the Lord, they fed many hungry people with a little bread during a famine.
But the beginning of this grace was seen in Zachariah's childhood, when he was a shepherd of lambs in the land of Klarjeti.
Acting as a priest, he prepared an offering before the honored cross. Other small children stood around him and cried out the song of the angels in unceasing voices, like this:
"Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of hosts. Heaven and earth are full of his glory. Alleluia, alleluia. Glory to God."
And they said "Kyrie eleison" a great many times. A pillar of very brilliant light had come down from heaven onto that innocent boy priest.

A bishop of Ancha who was travelling by saw that miracle. He went over and received communion from the hand of that worthy boy, then took the boy with him to Ancha, and he told the archpriest that he had received communion from him.
By that bishop's command, worthy men at Tbeti raised the blessed bishop Zachariah.
Such were the good virtues that the bishops of Ancha had as their inheritance.
But among that holy wheat one man was found who was like a tare that had sprung up in [?],
…in the diaconate, and raised in Tbilisi by the emir Sahak, son of Ishmael. He was travelling as an envoy to Ashot the kouropalates when he learned that the bishop of Ancha had died.
And because God, who is endlessly long-suffering, allowed it, that wicked Tsqiri used the emir Sahak's help to ask Ashot the kouropalates for the see of Ancha.
And when he had taken Ancha by force, he went on to add many more evils to his evil. It is not fitting to write all of them down in this book.
